items.text:
German auto workers on back foot as costs, competition bite
November 25, 2026
For decades, German auto bosses and labor representatives touted their ability to work through their disagreements in a uniquely cooperative process. Those days appear to be gone.
A series of crises across the industry and abrupt moves by management to slash costs are testing the limits of the German power-sharing agreement.
As negotiations between union representatives and Germany's largest carmaker, Volkswagen, began on Tuesday, the balance of power appeared increasingly one-sided.
Volkswagen wants to freeze wages for the next two years while cutting several allowances and bonuses.
Alongside Mercedes, it's demanding longer hours under the same pay, with both companies threatening to withhold investment from German factories.
Unions have responded with warning strikes and the threat of larger walkouts. Yet workers are aware of the grim outlook, with Germany's auto industry losing more than 123,000 jobs between 2019 and 2025, according to the Ifo Institute.
"I think that the labor representatives are in a very difficult situation," said Thomas Haipeter, a labor researcher at the University of Duisburg-Essen. "On the one hand, they have to make concessions in order to safeguard jobs. And despite these massive employment reductions to safeguard the rest of the jobs and locations, what is missing for them is a kind of more offensive strategy."
A hot shower a day
Labor's outsized role in German auto companies goes back decades and includes a 1945 deal at Volkswagen promising a hot shower a day.
That year marks the start of "co-determination" at the company, in which workers are represented internally by employee-led workers' councils, as well as by outside labor unions.
Berlin then anchored labor's strong say in Volkswagen in 1960, before the firm issued public shares, ensuring government officials retained extra votes in the supervisory board. Those seats, belonging to the Lower Saxony government, tend to be sympathetic to workers.
Workers' councils, meanwhile, became a fixture across the German auto industry, with representation extending across multiple production sites within the same companies.
Pay and benefits for auto workers have risen over the years. During the last German industry boom, between 2011 and 2019, pay for auto workers clearly outpaced the average German wage.
In early 2025, auto workers were earning nearly a third more per hour than the typical German worker, when bonuses and allowances are factored in, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
That same year, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume praised cooperation with the unions as one of the company's "great strengths” during the 80-year anniversary of the 1945 agreement.
Cracks in the relationship
Cracks were long in the making, according to case studies by Haipeter and others. Labor was increasingly forced to protect plants and jobs as companies chased cheaper workers abroad.
Workers' councils turned their attention to saving their own production lines. They focused on business strategy and even hired business consultants in an effort to sway strategy.
When combustion engines dominated, autoworkers could argue German production was the most technologically advanced, according to Haipeter. That changed with the shift to electric vehicles.
"This line of compromise is canceled now by management," he said. "They say it doesn't matter for us where we produce. We have to produce at the locations or in countries which are best-cost countries and not in countries which have higher wages."
Slow sales of electric autos and competition from Chinese manufacturers have, meanwhile, exposed the cost difference.
In 2024, Volkswagen abruptly canceled a series of labor agreements and threatened factory closures. After tough negotiations, labor agreed to significant cuts — €1.5 billion yearly in abandoned wage hikes and the elimination of 50,000 positions through attrition — in exchange for job security for current employees through 2030.
Management returned this summer with a restructuring plan that included the closures of four German plants. It delayed that decision following negotiations, but slated another 50,000 positions for attrition.
Volkswagen declined to comment for this article.
More hours, same pay
The most sensitive issue for unions may be the demand that employees work more for the same amount of pay, or even receive less for less work.
The union IG Metall won the concession for a 35-hour workweek in 1984 after seven weeks of strikes. It's now standard in every labor contract in the auto industry, although it's not uncommon for worksites to deviate upon employee agreement, according to Haipeter.
Mercedes has called for employees to agree to an exception across the company. The company acknowledged that the 35-hour workweek was "hard-won" and "means a great deal" to its workers. "However, the conditions under which it was agreed upon no longer exist today," it said in a statement to DW.
Volkswagen, meanwhile, is demanding greater "flexibility" as the negotiations get underway.
"They call it flexibility in both directions," Thorsten Gröger, head of negotiations for the union said last week. "In the end, Volkswagen wants its employees to perform unpaid work."
The 35-hour workweek is too sacred for unions to give in, said Ferdinand Dudenhöffer, a longtime analyst of the German car industry.
"The unions are in a difficult position," he noted. "They battled for a 35-hour workweek, and that's an incredible privilege that comes with a lot of pride. The union knows that as soon as one factory, one production hall, gives up the 35-hour workweek, then they will have a conflagration."
Düdenhöffer sees parallels in another crisis from Volkswagen's history. After a downturn in the early 1990s, the then-head of the German state of Lower Saxony, Gerhard Schröder, pushed for an agreement for workers to work less in exchange for retaining their job

items.text:
Germany news: Steinmeier arrives in Kenya for final leg of Africa tour
Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026
What you need to know
- President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is in Kenya for the final leg of his Africa tour
- A plaque for the Holocaust survivor Margot Friedländer is being unveiled in Berlin
- Protests are planned for the visit of ex-Mossad chief David Barnea in Berlin
Keep reading for the latest news and analysis from Germany on Wednesday, November 25:
German growth revised down for 3rd quarter
German GDP only grew by 0.1% between July and September, according to updated data from the Federal Statistics Offices (Destatis).
This marked a downwards revision from the 0.2% that had previously been estimated.
"After Germany's economic performance was robust in the first six months of the year in the face of geopolitical crises, economic growth slowed in the third quarter," statistics chief Ruth Brand said .
Despite a surprisingly good performance in the first half of the year, a slump in exports, as well as summer heatwaves and record-low water levels in rivers that hindered transportation of goods along Germany's key waterways, brought a slowdown to Europe's biggest economy.
Nevertheless, overall growth for the year is expected to reach its highest level since 2022 thanks to increased public spending on defense and infrastructure.
Protests planned over appearance of ex-Mossad chief at Bundestag breakfast
The former head of Israel's spy agency Mossad, David Barnea, is scheduled to take part in a breakfast meeting with members of the German parliament, the Bundestag, where he will discuss the ongoing war in the Middle East.
By his own admission, Barnea played a role in the pager attack that targeted members of Hezbollah in Lebanon in September 2024. The attack killed at least 37 people and injured some 300 others, including civilians. It has been described as a possible war crime by UN human rights chief Volker Türk.
That's why the human rights organization European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights (ECCHR) has called for Barnea's arrest, saying it filed a complaint with the Federal Prosecutor's Office.
"Germany must not provide a platform for alleged war criminals. Anyone who distributes thousands of everyday objects rigged with explosives and detonates them months later — without knowing where they will be at the time of detonation — knowingly accepts that an uncontrollable number of civilians will be injured or killed," ECCHR's Alexander Schwarz said.
Criticism also came from the Green party, with Bundestag member Kassem Taher Saleh saying Barnea had "no place in the Bundestag," in comments to the taz, due to the allegations against him. However, his Green colleague Konstantin von Notz defended the invitation, pointing to the close cooperation between Mossad and Germany's own intelligence agency.
Neither the Israeli government nor Barnea have commented on the ECCHR complaint.
Steinmeier to meet with Kenyan President Ruto in Nairobi
Following stops in the Ivory Coast and Ghana, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has arrived in Kenya for the final leg of his Africa tour.
He is set to meet with Kenyan President William Ruto to discuss bilateral relations, including economic cooperation. Kenya is one of Germany's main partners on the African continent. Following Kenya's independence from Britain in 1963, Germany was the first country to officially recognize it.
During his stay in the Ghanaian capital Accra, where he took part in the opening of the German-African Business Summit, Steinmeier called on German companies to engage more deeply in African countries.
In Kenya, the German president is set to visit the special economic zone of Tatu City, where a special tax priveleges are attracting businesses.
Steinmeier last visited Kenya in 2020, but this trip is likely to be his last, with his term ending in March 2027.
Welcome to our coverage
Good morning from chilly Bonn, where the cold weather has yet to bring any snow.
We will continue to bring you the latest from President Steinmeier's tour of Africa which will continue on Thursday in Kenya for the final leg.
We will also be following news out of Berlin where a plaque is set to be unveiled in memory of Holocaust survivor Margot Friedländer and where, separately, protests are planned against the arrival of former Mossad chief David Bernea.
For all this and more, keep reading.

items.title: All hostages freed after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
items.summary:
Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena, ending a day-long hostage siege, with the president saying all of those held have been rescued and one captor killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 peo
items.text:
Colombian security forces have stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena, ending a day-long hostage siege, with the president saying all of those held have been rescued and one captor killed.
Several explosions were heard before security forces entered the building, where about 20 people were believed to be being held by armed men.
The president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said: “In an extraordinary joint operation between the national police and the armed forces, all the hostages were rescued.”
Shortly after midnight on Wednesday, a police helicopter was hovering low over the shopping centre as security forces massed outside the supermarket. Explosions then echoed around the complex as tactical teams moved in.
Ten of an estimated 30 people that were initially held had already been released during the 17-hour standoff, including several elderly women.
Moments later, soldiers could be seen inside the Exito supermarket as security forces secured the building.
De la Espriella, who appeared at the scene wearing fatigues and with a sidearm and walkie-talkie, described the operation as a roaring success. He said: “We gave them the opportunity to surrender and free the hostages. They rejected that opportunity and we acted decisively.”
He said one hostage-taker had been killed.
Cartagena’s mayor said all the hostages were “safe and sound” and would reunite with their families before having medical checks.
The siege gripped Cartagena, a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism. Supermarket employees had been among those feared trapped inside.
“My son is there,” Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers, said earlier in the standoff. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him.”
Images broadcast by Colombian media and shared online appeared to show masked gunmen in tactical gear alongside zip-tied hostages inside the store.
De la Espriella was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups. “It’s not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping – no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people,” he said.
Authorities said the siege began after an attempted robbery on an armoured vehicle at the shopping centre.
According to local media, the hostage-takers were demanding nearly $2m (£1.5m), two armoured vehicles and safe passage to the city of Barranquilla, about 80 miles (130km) north-east of Cartagena. AFP could not independently verify those reports.
The siege unfolded on the 10th anniversary of Colombia’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas and a series of attacks across the country. Despite the deal to end the region’s largest insurgency, dissident guerrilla groups and criminal organisations still fight for control of parts of the country.
On Monday, authorities blamed a dissident Farc faction for a car bomb attack in the city of Villavicencio that wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.
Separately, the presidency said a “terrorist attack” on electrical infrastructure had disrupted power supplies in several south-western departments and prompted additional measures to protect energy facilities.

items.summary:

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the hospital
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) has announced a phased payment plan to settle outstanding staff dues as it engages unions over concerns surrounding payroll deductions, pension benefits and interest accrued on unpaid amounts.
In a statement issued on Wednesday, the hospital said the first payment was scheduled for Friday, with the next phase set for December 8.
The announcement comes amid industrial action by hospital staff, with management acknowledging concerns raised by employees over outstanding financial obligations.
KNH said it had begun taking steps to address the issues, including settling outstanding dues in phases.
The hospital confirmed that its first engagement with unions was held on Tuesday, November 24, with a follow-up meeting scheduled for Wednesday, November 25, to discuss the concerns and resolve other outstanding issues.
Management said it recognised employees as its greatest asset and remained committed to their welfare, professional growth and financial well-being.
“The Hospital acknowledges the concerns raised regarding unremitted payroll deductions, access to pension benefits and interest accrued on outstanding deductions,” the statement signed by Acting Chief Executive Officer Dr Joel Lassan said.
KNH appealed to staff to resume duty as discussions continue, saying cooperation and dialogue would help secure an amicable resolution while ensuring uninterrupted healthcare services.
The hospital said continued industrial action could affect thousands of patients who depend on its services, urging employees and unions to work with management towards resolving the dispute.
Management reiterated its commitment to providing a supportive working environment where employees feel valued and heard.

Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage crisis.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said all hostages had been rescued and one of the host
items.text:
Colombian security forces storm supermarket, free hostages
November 25, 2026
Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, ending a day-long hostage crisis.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said all hostages had been rescued and one of the hostage-takers had been killed.
"In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," de la Espriella said.
Around 30 people had initially been taken captive at a branch of the Exito supermarket chain in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood.
Ten of them, including some elderly women, had already been released on Tuesday after hours of negotiations.
No further details were immediately available about whether any of the hostages had been injured.
How did the Cartagena hostage crisis unfold?
According to authorities, the hostage crisis followed a failed attempt to rob an armored vehicle transporting cash from a shopping mall.
Police, troops and special forces were deployed to the supermarket as authorities sought to secure the release of the hostages.
Images circulating on social media appeared to show people kneeling inside the supermarket with their hands bound. The images could not be independently verified.
Supermarket employees were among those believed to have been taken hostage.
"My son is there," Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers, told news agency AFP during the standoff.
"He didn't leave work and he's not answering his phone. I think they took it from him," he said.
The supermarket chain said it was following the guidance of the authorities.
"For Grupo Exito, protecting the people's lives and safety is our priority," the company said in a statement.
The incident also temporarily disrupted air traffic in Cartagena, a Caribbean port known for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise ship tourism.
Arrivals at the city's Rafael Nunez airport were suspended for around 45 minutes in connection with the security operation.
What did Colombia's president say about the hostage crisis?
De la Espriella traveled to Cartagena on Tuesday, where he met commanders from a specialist anti-kidnapping and anti-extortion unit.
The president, who appeared in military fatigues, had previously expressed confidence that the captives would be freed.
"This is going to turn out well for the hostages," he said before arriving in Cartagena. "I'm not so sure it's going to turn out so well for the criminals."
De la Espriella ruled out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups in the incident.
Local media reported that the hostage-takers had made financial demands and requested safe passage to Barranquilla, another city on Colombia's Caribbean coast. Those reports could not be independently verified.
What is the security situation in Colombia?
Security has deteriorated across much of Colombia despite the tough rhetoric of its right-wing president, who took office in August.
On Monday, a car bombing in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio wounded 25 people and caused extensive damage.
The government blamed the attack on a faction of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels that rejects a 2016 peace agreement.
De la Espriella had visited Villavicencio following the bombing before traveling to Cartagena.
According to a Defense Ministry document shared with AFP, armed groups carried out 358 drone attacks between January and November — an average of more than one attack per day.

items.summary:
Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi attacks after Hodeidah strike
The escalation comes after the Yemeni rebel group threatened to attack the kingdom’s Red Sea ports if Saudi forces bombed port city.
Saudi Arabia says its air defences have intercepted several drones launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebel
items.text:
Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi attacks after Hodeidah strike
The escalation comes after the Yemeni rebel group threatened to attack the kingdom’s Red Sea ports if Saudi forces bombed port city.
Saudi Arabia says its air defences have intercepted several drones launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, a day after the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government carried out an air strike on the rebel-held port city of Hodeidah.
The coalition’s spokesman Turki Al-Maliki said that Saudi air defence systems destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia’s east on Wednesday morning, adding that fragments fell due to the interception, with no casualties reported in the initial assessment.
Al-Maliki said earlier that three drones were also shot down in the Eastern province.
The interceptions came after the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, said it had struck Yemen’s Hodeidah.
The Houthi armed group earlier threatened to retaliate against the kingdom’s Red Sea ports, including Jeddah in the event of an attack.
In a statement issued by Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree, the Iran-aligned rebel group urged employees and workers at the ports, as well as people nearby, to evacuate immediately and called on shipping companies to withdraw their vessels.
The attacks are the latest further escalation in the confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with attacks increasingly targeting strategic infrastructure on both sides.
On Tuesday, a Houthi drone struck the tallest tower in Riyadh, injuring at least 11 people, according to Saudi authorities.
Qatar and Pakistan, which have been mediating efforts to end the wider war in the region between Iran and the United States, both “strongly” condemned the attack on the tower, which houses the Saudi sovereign wealth fund.
The building had already been attacked last Thursday and is one of several high-profile targets hit since fighting with the Iran-backed Yemeni group reignited in July.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis promised a firm response to the attack.
Saudi attack on Hodeidah
The Saudi-led coalition targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah and destroyed several targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada and Amran, al-Maliki said.
Hodeidah, on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, is the main port through which food and other essential supplies enter Houthi-controlled northern Yemen.
It has long served as a key entry point for humanitarian aid and commercial imports, making it a lifeline for millions of Yemenis in a country heavily dependent on imported food.
Renewed fighting between the two sides has intensified since the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports in July. In September, the Iran-aligned group launched a lightning offensive, seizing territory from Yemeni government forces near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a strategic shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Yemeni government forces launched a counteroffensive last month, reclaiming some territory as fighting continues to rage on several fronts.
The Houthis have also stepped up strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, while Saudi Arabia has ramped up air strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen in response.

items.title: Countries that thrive on global cooperation must help sustain it
items.summary:
Countries that thrive on global cooperation must help sustain it
Prosperous small states like Qatar should combine their diplomatic and economic resources to advance international peace and stability.
“For thriving states, international peace and stability are not a luxury. They are the foundation o
items.text:
Countries that thrive on global cooperation must help sustain it
Prosperous small states like Qatar should combine their diplomatic and economic resources to advance international peace and stability.
“For thriving states, international peace and stability are not a luxury. They are the foundation of our national stories.”
Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani made this point at the Oxford Union earlier this month. For countries such as Qatar, prosperity rests on connections extending far beyond their borders. Energy exports, shipping routes and overseas investments depend on international predictability. Their security policy has to reflect that.
The meeting of the presidents of the United States, China and Russia – Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin – in Shenzhen on November 19 brought the problem into focus. Their declaration covered nuclear risks, energy supplies and reform of the United Nations. These are matters that affect every country. A few powers retain disproportionate influence over the outcome.
Dialogue among these powers is welcome. We should, however, have no illusions that their willingness to sit together signals the end of their competition. They can reach agreements while continuing to contest influence and access to resources. For countries outside the room, the consequences may arrive through a disrupted shipping route, a new restriction on trade or a security decision they had no part in making.
The prime minister’s concept of thriving states offers a way to think about their response. He described agile, stable and prosperous countries that have built influence beyond their size. Economic strength, adaptable institutions and trusted relationships give them room to act. Their exposure to decisions taken elsewhere gives them a reason to act together. Economic importance is no guarantee of security.
Thriving states can also help bridge the gaps between competing great powers. By maintaining diplomatic and economic ties with all sides, they can keep channels open when relations deteriorate. This gives them room to facilitate dialogue, support conflict resolution and identify areas where rivals still have an interest in cooperating.
The familiar classifications are of limited help here. The Global North and the Global South tell us little about which countries can work together on a particular problem. Developed and developing say something about economic conditions, but much less about diplomatic reach or the ability to support a peace process. A country may be small in population and still possess capabilities that larger states need.
Negotiations still have to take place. Aid needs access, ceasefires need monitoring, and agreements need someone to keep working on them after the announcement. Thriving states should take greater responsibility for this work. Their diplomatic access and financial resources are increasingly necessary to sustain functions that international institutions struggle to perform consistently.
Qatar is already doing this through its mediation between Washington and Tehran and its work on implementing the Gaza agreement. The limits of these efforts are visible. Agreements are violated, talks stall and violence continues. Maintaining a channel nevertheless preserves the possibility of a negotiated outcome. That channel has to survive setbacks if it is to be useful when an opening appears.
At Oxford, the prime minister pointed to Qatar’s cooperation with Norway and Switzerland on the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Such partnerships bring different relationships and experience to mediation. They offer a practical basis for cooperation among states that share an interest in a settlement, even when their wider foreign policies differ.
Regional organisations remain essential. In eastern DRC, Qatari facilitation of negotiations between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 rebel alliance has worked alongside efforts by the African Union, the US and Switzerland. Continued fighting and limited implementation show how much remains to be done. Thriving states should strengthen these partnerships and support the regional institutions involved.
The work also requires money and a longer view of what makes peace last. Preliminary OECD figures put Qatar’s official development assistance in 2025 at more than $900m. Restoring services, supporting institutions and creating economic opportunities are all critical for the settlement of conflicts. People need to see that an agreement changes something in their lives.
Commercial investment matters for a related reason. A 2025 Federal Reserve staff study documented how foreign direct investment is fragmenting along ideological and geographical lines. A government seeking finance for infrastructure or technology increasingly has to consider the strategic dependencies that may accompany it. Control of a port or a critical supply chain can give an outside power influence well beyond the original investment.
Thriving states have an opportunity to offer investment with fewer demands for geopolitical alignment. For a country with limited coercive reach and an economy dependent on international exchange, keeping markets open may be more valuable than drawing other countries into an exclusive sphere of influence. The benefit to recipients is greater choice over both their economic partners and their foreign policy.
That difference has to be demonstrated. Thriving states have interests, and their investments also generate influence.
The next step is to organise sustained cooperation among willing thriving states. Their economies are already connected through trade and investment. Their diplomatic cooperation should acquire comparable depth. A standing partnership would allow them to combine capabilities around particular problems while retaining their own priorities. Agreement on every international dispute is an unrealistic condition for useful work.

items.title: Is Russia really aiming for a new European security architecture?
items.summary:
Is Russia really aiming for a new European security architecture?
Moscow is piling on new demands in talks with Ukraine either as a negotiating strategy or as a diversion.
How do you stop the Ukraine war after nearly five years of bloodshed and destruction? The administration of United States Presid
items.text:
Is Russia really aiming for a new European security architecture?
Moscow is piling on new demands in talks with Ukraine either as a negotiating strategy or as a diversion.
How do you stop the Ukraine war after nearly five years of bloodshed and destruction? The administration of United States President Donald Trump seems to believe the path forward is mediation between Moscow and Kyiv.
Earlier this month, it restarted three-way talks with a meeting in Abu Dhabi. But instead of some outline of a deal, what we got was Russia adding yet another item of disagreement by bringing up European security architecture.
To stop pounding Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure, Russia is demanding far-reaching concessions by both the US and Europe. The wish-list includes NATO withdrawing forces from allies on the eastern flank and committing not to accept new members.
At some level, there is nothing new about the Russian demands. In December 2021, weeks before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia presented the US and NATO with two draft treaties which spelled out similar conditions.
The US rejected the far-reaching demands, which included scrapping NATO’s open-door policy, rolling back defence infrastructure and deployments in the east to the levels of 1997, and withdrawing US nuclear arms from Europe. Yet Washington was ready to engage on certain issues, including negotiations on intermediate and short-range missiles stationed in Europe, as well as transparency, risk reduction, and arms control.
Future historians may argue whether the acceptance of the entire package would have averted the war. But Russia’s ambition to recast the European security and political order was already there, in stark display, in late 2021. Ever since, Moscow has stuck to its guns – repeating at every twist and turn that “the root causes” of the conflict have to be addressed in a settlement.
One might agree or disagree about the merits of Russia’s perspective – blaming the war fully on the US and NATO and portraying its own actions as purely defensive. However, there is no denying how radical a cure the Kremlin prescribes to the alleged ills of Western expansion.
One would think that the failure to subdue Ukraine would have injected a dose of realism. A de facto partition of Ukrainian territory, with a ceasefire freezing the front lines, and gradual lifting of Western sanctions, is fully within Putin’s grasp. That is the message he is getting from both Trump and European leaders.
But at least officially, the Kremlin is having none of it. Instead, it is piling up new conditions: the cessation of European military support for Kyiv, no deployment of forces on Ukrainian soil, Finland exiting NATO and reverting to neutrality, prohibition of Ukraine’s participation in the European Union’s budding defence initiatives, no extension of the British and French nuclear umbrella to their European allies, etc.
In other words, nearly all gains Europe has made since February 2022 in terms of strengthening its collective defence have to go in order for Russia to stop fighting. It seems Putin’s ambitions know no bounds.
Obviously, such an overhaul of European security arrangements is, to put it politely, not very likely. Even Trump, however eager he might be to cut a deal with “his friend” Putin, will not be willing, much less able, to deliver Europe on a silver platter.
Ukraine will not stop fighting – it made that abundantly clear with the successful strikes against the Kerch bridge and Russian ships in the Baltic and off Libya’s coast in the Mediterranean. Nor will Europe – for all the uncertainty about funding and the rise of Ukraine-sceptical parties and leaders in key countries – stop supporting Kyiv.
The Russian side is fully aware of the limits and constraints, and yet it hammers on with the same talking points over and over again. The question is why.
The more benign interpretation of Russia’s overly ambitious demands has to do with basic negotiation strategy. Russia is setting a very high asking price in order to extract as much as is realistically possible in the talks with the US and the Europeans.
Once the guns fall silent, there will be practical issues of managing the Cold War-like standoff between NATO and Russia as well as between a Western-backed Ukraine and Russia. Some guardrails would probably be welcomed by both sides on transparency of troop and equipment movements and joint exercises.
There could be military-to-military dialogue or an open line between security and intelligence agencies. It is even possible that there could be some common understandings on hybrid warfare – acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and the like, which have recently been on the rise.
Trying to prevent and/or manage escalation through a new security regime could be possible. The Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), in which both EU member states and Russia participate, could get a new lease of life in such a scenario.
A return to summits involving Russia, on one side, and the US and major European countries on the other might also be a possibility, especially after Putin is gone.
The more sceptical interpretation of Russia’s demands is that it is trying to dilute the agenda and in effect divert attention away from Ukraine in order to gain extra advantage on the battlefield.
In Moscow’s thinking, strategic-level relations between great powers have priority over regional issues. Vladimir Medinsky, Putin’s aide and chief negotiator, put it bluntly: “Essentially, the whole body is sick, and in the Ukraine, there was just a cyst that burst.”

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – Kenya and Israel have launched a goat and sheep training centre in Kiambu County to help farmers improve livestock breeding, animal nutrition and productivity through practical training and modern agricultural technologies.
The centre, located at 27 Farms, was launched on Monday through a partnership between the farm and Israel’s Agency for International Development Cooperation (MASHAV).
Speaking during the launch, Israeli Ambassador to Kenya Gideon Behar described the facility as a milestone in agricultural cooperation between the two countries.
“I think this is another milestone in the very long cooperation between Israel and Kenya in the field of agriculture,” Behar said.
The centre will offer practical training in dairy goat and sheep farming, animal genetics and feed production. It is also equipped with a feed pellet-making machine provided through MASHAV to help farmers improve livestock nutrition and manage feed supplies, particularly during dry periods.
Training is expected to begin in early 2027.
Behar said the facility was the first Israeli-supported training centre in Kenya dedicated specifically to goats and sheep. He expressed hope that it would become a model for similar initiatives in other parts of the country.
“This is a center of excellence, first-class activities in goats and sheep farming, and with Israeli assistance and local knowledge, I’m sure that we can spread more and more knowledge and more and more bring into the countryside and into the hands of the small farmers the knowledge of modern agriculture,” he said.
He said improving livestock breeds and farming practices was increasingly important as climate change, population growth and shrinking agricultural land put pressure on food production.
Israel’s contribution, he added, would focus on transferring agricultural knowledge, building farmers’ skills and providing technical support.
Behar also disclosed that Kenya’s Ministry of Agriculture was considering introducing the Assaf sheep breed from Israel, which he said could produce about five litres of milk a day. He said the ministry had started planning for the proposed introduction, with Israel expected to provide technical assistance.
He further indicated that another Israeli-supported training centre focusing on beekeeping was expected to be launched before the end of the year.
Peter Njenga, Deputy Director of Livestock Production at the State Department for Livestock Development, who represented the Principal Secretary, said improving animal genetics was essential to raising livestock productivity and meeting growing food demand.
Njenga, who works in animal genetic resource conservation, said selective breeding enables farmers to develop animals with desirable traits, including faster growth, greater body weight and increased milk production.
“Conservation of our animal genetics is very, very important in this country because it is through conserving and improving on those genetics that we are able to increase the production of those animals,” he said.
He said farmers could produce more food from smaller pieces of land by improving the productivity of individual animals rather than relying mainly on increasing livestock numbers.
However, he cautioned that efforts to improve breeds should not undermine the conservation of indigenous animal genetic resources, which carry traits that could be valuable for future breeding programmes.
“One negative aspect of improving production or improving the genetics is you continuously lose some very important traits. And these traits we also need to conserve them,” he said.
Njenga said the government operates 15 centres across the country dedicated to conserving indigenous animal breeds. He added that genetic improvement requires substantial financial investment, specialised expertise and time.
Kiambu County Chief Officer for Livestock, Fisheries and Veterinary Services John Kuria, who represented Governor Kimani Wamatangi, said the centre could help address challenges facing livestock farmers in the county, particularly the high cost and poor quality of animal feeds.
“One of our greatest challenges in livestock production in Kiambu is low quality of the feeds, coupled with high cost,” Kuria said.
He said the county government would work with the farm to provide technical support and train farmers, drawing on the expertise of county livestock officers.
“Through their cooperation, we will also be collaborating with the farm to train our farmers,” he said.
Kuria noted that the county was already supporting livestock production through programmes targeting women and young people and would seek to expand its focus on goat breeding and production.
MASHAV representative and agricultural expert Eitan Hatzor said the centre was developed following engagement with the farm’s management, which began during a goat farming course in Israel about two years ago.
Hatzor said animal feeds account for an estimated 60 to 70 per cent of livestock production costs, making efficient feed management critical to improving farmers’ returns.
He said the pellet-making machine would allow the farm to combine different feed ingredients into pellets designed to provide balanced nutrition for goats and sheep.
The equipment is also expected to support feed production for farmers in the surrounding area.
Jacqueline Gathura, Director of 27 Farms and a beneficiary of MASHAV agricultural training in Israel, said the farm had been working to improve its dairy goat and sheep breeds through selective breeding and the introduction of other genetic lines.
She said the farm initially focused on dairy goats before expanding into meat goat and sheep production. It currently keeps dairy goats, Boer goats for meat production and sheep, including crosses developed from indigenous Red Maasai sheep and Meatmaster breeding stock from South Africa.

items.text:
From stargazing to space: Pakistan watches its first astronaut take flight
Students and stargazers packed SUPARCO’s auditorium before dawn to watch Zeeshan Ali reach orbit on a Chinese rocket.
Islamabad, Pakistan — It was 5:18am (00:18 GMT) on Wednesday, before dawn in a chilly Islamabad. On the screen at the front of the auditorium, a Chinese rocket carrying Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, Pakistan’s first astronaut, rose on a column of orange flames.
As the rocket lifted off, Pakistan’s national anthem began. The audience, which had been slouching in their seats, rose row by row and sang along.
While many took out their phones to record the historic moment, Zainab Abbasi’s eyes remained fixed on the giant screen.
“I had my phone out to record it on video, but I was so caught up in the moment that I forgot to record, and I was just standing there with my phone closed,” Abbasi, 21, told Al Jazeera.
A second-year undergraduate student of physics and astronomy at the National University of Sciences and Technology (NUST), Abbasi was with her friends in the auditorium at the headquarters of the Pakistan Space & Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO).
As the rocket climbed higher, the hall erupted in applause and chants of “Pakistan Zindabad” (“Long live Pakistan”).
The Long March-2F rocket lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China, carrying Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, alongside Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan Air Force pilot.
But within two minutes of liftoff, the hall fell silent. No one spoke. Faces across the rows were tense. On the screen, the rocket had shrunk to a dot.
“There was, I think, anticipation and also, for me specifically, a sort of, you know, underlying anxiety,” Abbasi told Al Jazeera.
On January 28, 1986, the US space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff, killing all seven crew members.
About 10 minutes after Wednesday’s launch, the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft separated from the rocket and entered orbit, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA).
The silence lasted several minutes, until one of the hosts congratulated the audience on a successful launch. People got up, greeted one another or headed for the doors.
A few hours later, CMSA and SUPARCO confirmed that the spacecraft had docked at China’s Tiangong space station at 8:56am (03:56 GMT). The crew were expected to enter the station at about 11:45am (06:45 GMT).
A hall before dawn
The auditorium had been packed by 5am (00:00 GMT). Those unable to find a seat sat on the floor or stood along the walls.
Tayyaba Riaz, a final-year mathematics student at NUST, said every seat was taken when she arrived at about 4:20am (23:20 GMT Tuesday). Originally from Chitral in Pakistan’s northwest, she lives in a university hostel.
When she asked hostel authorities to leave early in the morning, she said they asked where she was going. “I was like, ‘I am going to witness a history,’” she said, giggling.
Many in the auditorium held glossy cards bearing Ali’s portrait in a spacesuit and the words “Pakistan’s First Manned Space Mission”. Paper flags of Pakistan and China rested on laps, while green and white balloons lined the stage.
The screen carried a livestream of the launch. There was a brief moment of hilarity when, just before liftoff, a YouTube advertisement appeared, causing mild panic that the critical moment might be missed.
‘It will never be us’
Abbasi, the second-year student, had been at SUPARCO since 2am (21:00 GMT Tuesday). She lives 40km (25 miles) away and had left home at 7pm (14:00 GMT) on Tuesday to spend the night at her aunt’s house nearby.
She is a member of PakAstronomers, a group of amateur astronomers in Islamabad. Her interest in astronomy began around 2018, when she was 13, after the cartoon series Beyblade introduced her to constellations.
Her family, particularly her father, has always supported her, even if they do not always understand her passion, she said.
“When I was a child and interested in space, becoming an astronaut felt like a far-off dream only available to a child in America and not in Pakistan,” she said.
Ahzam Farooq, a physics undergraduate at NUST and vice president of the society, used to wake at 3am to watch rocket launches.
“My parents used to ask, ‘What is there in this?’ like it will never be us,” he said.
Adan Athar, a second-year space sciences student at the Institute of Space Technology (IST) in Islamabad, is from Faisalabad and a founding member of the Faisalabad Astronomical Society.
She told Al Jazeera she was the first in her family to take an interest in space.
“Yes, they were very supportive, and they think I will be the next astronaut,” she said with a shy smile.
Fifty years of stargazing
But it is not only Pakistan’s youth following Ali’s journey.
Saif-ul-Islam Qureshi, a 72-year-old electronics engineer, has been watching the sky for at least 50 years.
“I was 12 years old when I started this hobby with my small binocular, and then my first observation was the Big Dipper in the sky,” he told Al Jazeera.
The Big Dipper is a group of seven bright stars whose two end stars point towards the North Star.
Qureshi helped found PakAstronomers, the group Abbasi belongs to. It was initially called the Pakistan Astronomy Society.
Its members took astronomy to schools, colleges, universities and public parks. Many people did not know planets could be seen with the naked eye, he said.
Over the past decade, however, that had changed. Even small children were now well informed.
“We were sensing that a storm was building. A storm is building, and a storm in a positive sense,” he said.
What comes next?
In a speech before the launch, SUPARCO chairman Muhammad Yousaf Khan said Pakistan was setting its sights further ahead.
“Our ambition is beyond just this launch. Our commitment is to reach the moon by 2035,” he said.
Speaking to Al Jazeera afterwards, Khan said the first step would be a lunar rover, due to fly in 2028.

items.text:
Rescuers search for dozens trapped in flooded Indonesia gold mine
Police say 26 workers are yet to be rescued from a mine that flooded when a nearby river overflowed after heavy rain.
Rescuers are searching for dozens of workers feared trapped in a flooded unauthorised mine in Indonesia’s West Java province, police and authorities said.
The open-pit gold mine in Java’s Bogor district was flooded when a nearby river overflowed after a torrential downpour on Monday, trapping the miners, police said on Wednesday.
“As of now, there were 26 people who have yet to be evacuated,” said West Java police spokesman Hendra Rochmawan in a statement.
The Jakarta Search and Rescue Office said the workers were stuck in a 100-metre (328-foot) deep mine. Access was narrow, and the terrain was slippery and dark, the agency added, giving no details of the size of the rescue operation or any progress made towards reaching the trapped miners.
“We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft,” Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement.
“The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely.”
The mine is located in the Pongkor area of Bogor, a mountainous area 60km south of the capital Jakarta, where state miner Antam runs gold-mining operations.
Small-scale and unauthorised mining ‌has often led to accidents in resource-rich Indonesia, where mineral resources are located in remote areas in conditions difficult for authorities to regulate.
Authorities closed ‌about ‌30 gold mine pits last week in a separate area in Bogor, news website Detik reported.

items.summary: Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly
items.text:
Pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, not long after the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to the finals of the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio.
Reporter Guillermo Blanco, who was writing about the meeting for Argentinian sports magazine El Gráfico, got the OK from Pelé’s people and was so intent on making it happen that he checked Maradona onto a flight one Sunday night without telling him. He collared the young man after Argentine Juniors played Huracán and then raced to the airport and put him on a plane with his father, his agent and a photographer.
The next day, the small group of Argentines went to Alfredo Saad’s apartment in Copacabana, where Maradona and Pelé sat for an hour discussing football and life. ‘It was all great, they chatted, Pelé got out his guitar, he sang some songs, it was really nice,’ Blanco recalled. ‘Then there was a moment when it got a bit deep when Pelé started to give Diego some advice. He took Diego’s hand and he started giving him counsel. “Look after your body. Remember to always train. There’s a lot of responsibility on your shoulders.” It was like a premonition. Everything that would happen to Diego, Pelé, with all his experience, was telling him would happen.’ Before they left, Pelé hugged Maradona’s father and gave his son a signed ball, a Brazil shirt and a Pelé watch. The friendship between the players appeared to be sealed. ‘I knew Pelé was a God as a player,’ Maradona said. ‘Now that I’ve met him, I know he is as a person, too.’
Those present that sunny afternoon in Rio could never have imagined how the paths of the two men would diverge, overlap and collide, like wingers and full-backs determined to get the better of each other. Their mutual admiration survived for a few more years but when it soured, it soured royally and the fallout made headlines around the world. They were often described as rivals but what they really had was a love-hate relationship fuelled by South American nationalism and grandiose egos. Adding even more spice were the moralistic subtexts of good vs evil, the establishment vs the people, and the conformist vs the rebel. They were two completely different people and everyone took a side. Maradona summed it up perfectly: ‘We’re oil and water.’
The first cracks in their friendship appeared three years after their Rio meeting, when Pelé criticised Maradona’s performance at the 1982 World Cup. The Brazilian agreed to write a syndicated column during the tournament, and before it even kicked off he predicted that Zico would make more of an impact than Maradona. In a sentence that would drive the first wedge between them, he questioned not just Maradona’s ability but his character. ‘My biggest doubt,’ Pelé wrote, ‘lies in knowing if Diego has sufficient greatness in his person to justify the honours that the world audience pays him.’
Pelé’s scepticism turned out to be entirely justified. Maradona lost the plot in Argentina’s second-round match against Brazil and was sent off after stamping on Batista in the dying minutes of their 3-1 loss. The defeat meant the champions were out and Maradona, as Pelé predicted, had failed to live up to the hype. In his column the next day, Pelé piled on the misery, calling Maradona ‘an immature young man, who almost hasn’t had the time to transform himself into the great player that many people blindly state that he is’.
To Maradona, the words were a betrayal. He had considered Pelé a friend and an ally, and he never forgot how the Brazilian became one of the first major figures to cast aspersions on his talent and character. Maradona was hardly a paragon of loyalty – he fought with just about everyone who ever loved him – but he demanded fealty from everyone else and Pelé’s slight wounded him deeply. And yet it took a while for his anger to show. Maradona was just 21 and a long way from becoming the all-conquering superstar who would wow the world. He had opinions but he was still shy about speaking out, not yet sure how good he would really be. It was only after leading Argentina to victory in 1986 that his ego exploded and he started reacting to his critics. It was then, after the world united in appointing him as the successor to Pelé’s throne, that he began assailing everyone who questioned his greatness.
It took a while, but Pelé saw what was happening and he realised he had to react. He began defending his legacy and the rivalry between the two men was up and running. For almost his entire career, Pelé was recognised as the greatest footballer of all time. Rivals had come and gone but none posed a lasting threat to the coveted title. Peers such as Alfredo Di Stéfano, Eusébio and Johan Cruyff all had the talent to threaten his supremacy but they and their supporting casts were either not good enough or not consistent enough to keep their teams at the top for extended periods, especially at international level.
Maradona was different and Pelé knew it. He wasn’t just brilliant, he also played for a nation that produced enough quality players to help him win the titles he needed to be considered extra-special. Crucially, like few players before or since, he had both an aura about him as well as a gift for making the players around him better. He never won anything single-handedly, as many people liked to say, but when he was on form his teammates grew in stature and together they became more than just the sum of their parts.
His performances in leading Argentina to the World Cup in 1986 were so remarkable that Pelé started playing up his own achievements and subtly questioning those of his rival. While the rest of the world marvelled at football’s new messiah, Pelé would grumpily ask how anyone could

items.title: Has a footballer had a longer career hiatus than Ronaldinho’s 11 year-gap? | The Knowledge
items.summary:
“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, earlier this month. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”
Ronaldinho’s last professional appearance
items.text:
“Ronaldinho played for Ravenna, in Serie C, earlier this month. It was his first professional appearance in more than 11 years,” writes George Jones. “Have any other footballers had long career hiatuses? And has any player had a longer hiatus than 11 years?”
Ronaldinho’s last professional appearance before his return for Ravenna came on 26 September 2015 for Fluminense, who won 2-0 at home against Goiás. He was withdrawn after 45 minutes. Fans of symmetry will be pleased to see that 11 years and 50 days later, the Brazilian returned for Ravenna in a 2-0 home win against another team with five letters and an accent in their name, Forlì, and was withdrawn after 45 minutes.
Considering he is now 46 and was playing against a team containing a couple of players 26 years his junior, his 25 touches, one key pass (in the buildup to the opening goal) and 81% passing accuracy in a single half is better than respectable. And nope, stats weren’t available for tracking back and we don’t imagine he ranked too highly on that metric … but he’s 46! Only time will tell if the World Cup winner plays again. “It was amazing,” he beamed after the match. “I got more than 30 minutes under my belt and feel good. I didn’t really want to come off. It was all over in a flash. I’m still not sure if this will be my only appearance, but if the president comes calling, I’ll be back.”
But back to the question. There have been a few high-profile returns following a player’s initial “retirement”. In 2012 Paul Scholes jumped back into Manchester United’s midfield seven months after hanging up his boots to help out amid an injury crisis and played for another 18 months, helping United to seal their 20th league title in May 2013. Arjen Robben resumed his career at his boyhood club, Groningen, a year after calling time at Bayern Munich.
A more curious example is that of the former Argentina goalkeeper Carlos Roa, who at his peak and aged 30, took a retreat from football to focus on his faith with reports suggesting he anticipated the year 2000 being the end of the world. A devout Christian, Roa went to live with his family in a secluded area of Argentina to prepare for the apocalypse. When it didn’t come, he resumed his career at Mallorca a year after his last appearance but never played for the national team again.
But these tales get us nowhere near to Ronaldinho. Gareth Barry had a four-and-a-half-year hiatus between his retirement as a professional at West Brom in 2020 and his return to playing again at Hurstpierpoint in the Mid Sussex League Championship in February 2025 – not at professional level but still pretty competitive. Jürgen Klinsmann made a similar return to playing at amateur level five years after “retiring”. Klinsmann scored on his farewell appearance for Tottenham in a 1-1 draw with Southampton on the last day of the 1997-98 Premier League season. However, aged 39, he came back under the pseudonym “Jay Göppingen” and scored five goals in eight appearances for Orange County Blue Star, a team in the Premier Development League (then the fourth tier of the US pyramid).
Maybe Ronaldinho was inspired by his former World Cup-winning teammate Denílson signing for Íbis Sport Club in 2022, 12 years after his retirement. However, the then 44-year-old never made an appearance for the lower-league Brazilian club, with the signing seemingly a publicity stunt for a club often dubbed the “worst in the world” after going three years, 11 months and 26 days without a win in the 1980s.
Which takes us to another brilliant Brazilian. The late, great Sócrates came out of retirement on 20 November 2004 aged 50, 15 years after his last appearance for Botafogo on 12 November 1989. He signed a one-month player-coach deal with Garforth Town, on the outskirts of Leeds, in the Northern Counties East Football League and played 12 minutes at the end of a 2-2 draw with Tadcaster Albion. “It was far too cold; the second I got out there I had an incredible headache. I’m just not used to it,” he gasped after the match. “But I really enjoyed it and it was an interesting experience.” His appearance drew huge crowds to tiny Wheatley Park and came about because of a shared interest in football coaching schools for children which the owner, Simon Clifford, was trying to promote.
The hiatus for Sócrates stands at 15 years and eight days, four years greater than that of Ronaldinho, though perhaps Ronaldinho’s ability to step back into the third tier of a professional league and more than hold his own is a more impressive achievement. What is unarguable, though, is their status as two Brazil greats.
The former Scotland defender Neil McBain had a playing hiatus longer than the two legends above, however. “McBain started his career as a half-back for Ayr United in 1915,” writes Robin Horton. “He retired in 1931, as player-manager for Watford, by which time he was playing centre-half, his last game being an FA Cup tie at Birmingham on 14 February. By 1946 he was in charge of New Brighton.”
“On 15 March 1947, with the club suffering a goalkeeping crisis, and with four players – including chosen keeper Corbett – failing to turn up for a match at Hartlepool United, McBain himself donned the green jersey. The Rakers duly lost 3–0, although the first goal was a shot ‘which might easily have caused Frank Swift’s eyes to boggle’. At 51 years old, he was the oldest player ever to play in the Football League – 16 years, one month and one day from his previous appearance.”
Drawing down

Leicester won the FA Cup in 2021, when Youri Tielemans scored a spectacular winner against Chelsea at Wembley in front of a post-Covid crowd of 20,000. For people who travel frequently, the journey is often as important as the destination. From navigating busy airports and finding a moment to relax before a flight to securing a dinner reservation in an unfamiliar city, convenience can make all the difference.
It is this lifestyle that I&M Bank is targeting with the introduction of its Mastercard World Elite Metal Credit Card, a premium offering designed for customers who value travel, experiences, convenience and personalised service.
The sleek metal card brings together a collection of travel and lifestyle privileges aimed at Kenya’s affluent professionals, executives and globally mobile clientele, giving cardholders access to benefits that extend well beyond everyday payments.
A more comfortable journey
For frequent flyers, airport time can be one of the less enjoyable parts of travelling. The World Elite Metal Card seeks to make it more comfortable by offering unlimited global airport lounge access for the cardholder and one guest.
Whether travelling for business or leisure, lounge access provides an opportunity to relax, enjoy refreshments or work in a quieter environment before boarding.
Cardholders will also enjoy fast-track airport services at select locations, helping make the airport experience smoother, particularly for those navigating busy international terminals.
A dedicated concierge service adds another layer of convenience, offering assistance with travel arrangements, dining reservations and lifestyle requests.
Experiences beyond the destination
The appeal of premium travel increasingly lies in the experiences people enjoy along the way.
Through Mastercard’s Priceless platform, World Elite cardholders can access curated experiences across dining, sports, culture and entertainment. These experiences are designed to connect customers with opportunities that go beyond conventional travel itineraries.
The card also provides access to curated hotel partnerships and lifestyle privileges across retail and hospitality, including golf programmes, luxury retail offers and selected hotel benefits.
For those who enjoy exploring new destinations, these partnerships can add another dimension to travel, whether through a hotel stay, a dining experience or access to a cultural or sporting event.
Premium service, wherever you are
Travelling internationally often means dealing with unfamiliar environments, changing plans and unexpected situations. I&M Bank’s World Elite offering includes comprehensive travel and medical insurance, emergency assistance, fraud monitoring, purchase protection and dedicated support for cardholders.
The combination of insurance, assistance and personalised support is designed to provide greater peace of mind when travelling or making purchases internationally.
The card also reflects the changing expectations of premium customers, who increasingly want financial services that fit seamlessly into their lifestyles.
No spending threshold to unlock the experience
One of the card’s standout features is that it comes with no minimum spending requirement to access its full range of benefits.
Eligible cardholders can enjoy the privileges from day one without having to meet a prescribed spending target to unlock the lifestyle offering.
That means the experience is built around the customer’s lifestyle and preferences rather than the amount they spend on the card.
A lifestyle statement
The Mastercard World Elite Metal Card is also designed to make a statement through its metal construction, combining durability with a premium aesthetic.
But beyond its physical appearance, its proposition is centred on what the card enables its holder to experience.
From airport lounges and concierge assistance to hotel privileges, dining, sporting and cultural experiences, the offering brings together a range of services aimed at making travel and everyday lifestyle experiences more rewarding.
For I&M Bank, the launch represents an expansion of its premium banking offering. For customers, it is an invitation to experience a more connected approach to banking, travel and lifestyle.
In an increasingly globalised world where people move between cities, countries and cultures with greater frequency, the value of a premium card may increasingly be measured not simply by what it pays for, but by the experiences, convenience and possibilities it opens up.

items.text:
Sentences served, but Gaza prisoners remain behind Israeli bars
Palestinian families in Gaza wait for loved ones who remain in Israeli prisons despite completing their sentences.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Fadi Zughra’s four children were excited in February when they heard that he’d finally been released from Israeli prison.
He’d been incarcerated since 2016 and completed an 8.5-year sentence in early 2025, but stayed locked up.
So when friends called up to say that Fadi, 43, was at southern Gaza’s Nasser Hospital, his children rushed to get ready to go and greet him.
But his wife, Shmou, hesitated and insisted that they had to verify with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) that he had actually been released.
She was right to double-check. Fadi was still in prison.
“I was shocked, and the girls were very upset. One of my daughters even fainted,” she said.
Fadi is among 48 prisoners from Gaza who remain in Israeli custody after completing their sentences, according to the Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs. Their continued detention raises questions about the legal grounds for holding them after their prison terms have expired.
Palestinian prisoners’ organisations say Israel has used its Unlawful Combatants Law to continue detaining Palestinians from Gaza.
Passed in 2002, the law allows the detention of people classified as “unlawful combatants” without a criminal conviction, subject to detention orders and judicial review.
Fadi was arrested on August 15, 2016, while fishing at sea, detained alongside other fishermen. He had worked as a fisherman since childhood.
“The first thing we heard was that he had been killed,” Shmou said. “After about three days, the Red Cross told us he was in prison.”
Fadi had been accused of smuggling and sabotage – allegations Shmou rejected, insisting that he was simply a fisherman trying to earn a living.
Sentences served, but no freedom
For Hanan Harara, the wife of another prisoner, Hisham Harara, the wait has also been marked by repeated hopes of reunion. Whenever news spreads of a prisoner release, she searches the lists for her husband’s name.
On one occasion, after hearing that a group of prisoners had arrived at Gaza’s European Hospital, Hanan and her children rushed there from Deir el-Balah, where they had been displaced. But he did not come home.
Her children have grown tired of the repeated disappointment.
“They tell me, ‘Mum, you keep checking the lists. We don’t want to look at them any more,’” Hanan said. “But I still check. I keep hoping that perhaps this time he will be among those released.”
Hisham completed a nine-year sentence in December 2024, but remains in Israeli custody. His wife said the family had counted down the days while displaced in southern Gaza, as a result of Israel’s ongoing genocidal war.
“But that date [of his release] passed, and we are still waiting,” Hanan said.
Hisham was arrested in December 2015, while travelling through the Beit Hanoon crossing (called Erez in Israel) between Israel and Gaza to reach Jenin in the occupied West Bank, where he worked. He operated heavy machinery and bulldozers, and had previously worked clearing rubble and demolishing buildings damaged during Israel’s 2014 war on Gaza.
Hanan said the allegations against him were related to tunnels, despite his work involving rubble removal and demolition above ground.
These cases come amid a wider rise in the number of Palestinians held in Israeli prisons and detention facilities.
B’Tselem has reported that the Israel Prison Service held 9,187 Palestinians on security grounds at the end of June 2026, including 1,554 from Gaza.
Palestinian prisoners’ institutions reported in October that more than 9,400 Palestinians were in Israeli custody, including 1,419 detainees from Gaza classified by Israel as “unlawful combatants”.
Conditions for Palestinians held in Israeli prisons have deteriorated since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, and the start of Israel’s war on Gaza on the same date.
The United Nations and human rights organisations have documented widespread torture, including beatings, starvation, and rape. The UN Human Rights Office said in September that it had verified the deaths of at least 92 Palestinians in Israeli custody since October 2023.
Children growing up without their fathers
For the families, the separation has become even harder since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began.
Shmou and her children – Almasa and Shahd, both 16, Lana, 14, and Sakher, 11 – used to visit Fadi roughly every two months. Their last visit was about six weeks before the war. Since then, she said, they have not had any news about him.
Sakher was around seven months old when his father was arrested, but grew attached to his father during the prison visits.
“When Sakher visited Fadi, he would tell him, ‘Dad, I want to do this’ and ‘Dad, I want to do that.’ His psychological state has been very difficult,” Shmou said.
Hanan has raised her seven children without Hisham. Their youngest daughter, Eileen, was a baby when he was arrested. She is now 12. Her eldest son, Amjad, was 18 at the time and is now 28.
“When Hisham was detained, I became both a mother and a father,” Hanan said.
No communication
Both women have also struggled to learn what their husbands know about the war and whether they are receiving information about their families.
Shmou said former prisoners sometimes pass messages from Fadi, telling her that he is alive and wants to know whether she and the children are safe.
But she worries about reports that detainees are sometimes given false information about the deaths of relatives.
“The Israelis tell him that his family has been killed, or that one of his children has been killed,” she said. “They play with his mental state and his nerves.”

Mugabe was arrested ear
items.text:
Zimbabwe issues arrest warrant for Robert Mugabe's son over missed court date
- Published
A Zimbabwean court has issued an arrest warrant for Bellarmine Chatunga Mugabe, the youngest son of the country's late former president Robert Mugabe, after he failed to appear in court.
Mugabe was arrested earlier this month alongside four others over assault allegations on a police officer during an investigation into the suspected smuggling of luxury vehicles.
The group subsequently faced charges of robbery and malicious damage to property. They have yet to enter pleas.
They were granted bail on 6 November and were due back in court on Tuesday. However, Mugabe failed to attend. His co-accused, an aide and three security guards appeared and were remanded until 10 December.
Prosecutors allege that Mugabe and the others assaulted an investigating officer using their hands and broomsticks.
The officer's phone was allegedly taken and smashed on the ground, while one of the accused is said to have seized the officer's loaded pistol.
Bellarmine Chatunga is the youngest son of Robert Mugabe and his second wife, Grace Mugabe.
Robert Mugabe ruled Zimbabwe for 37 years before being forced from power in 2017, aged 93, following a military intervention. He died in 2019.
His son has attracted public attention in recent years over a series of legal troubles and his high-profile lifestyle.
Last month, he admitted to drug-related charges involving the possession of cannabis.
In April, he was deported from neighbouring South Africa after pleading guilty to pointing a firearm and being in the country illegally. He had been arrested following the shooting of a 23-year-old man at his home.
In 2023, he was arrested in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, over allegations that he damaged property and spat at a police officer during a party.
He was later freed after reaching an out-of-court settlement with the complainant, who was a friend.
