items.text:
How to unearth young stars, the Bayern Munich way
- Published
Bayern Munich are one of the elite powers in European football and current home of Ballon d'Or winner and England captain Harry Kane.
But, while Kane is the latest hugely successful foreign import at Bayern, the German giants also put a particular focus on producing their own elite young talent.
In 2013, Bayern had four homegrown players in the starting line-up as they won the Champions League.
Repeating that victory, and continuing the club's history of nurturing young players, is what director of youth development and campus Jochen Sauer says Bayern are aiming for.
Sauer joined from Red Bull Salzburg in 2017 when the academy campus opened in another part of Munich, away from the first-team training complex.
The club's motto "Mia San Mia" translates to "we are who we are" and Sauer says it has always been the club's goal to have a local homegrown element in its senior side.
"It was always our identity and philosophy to be a regional club, but at the same time to be competitive internationally and on Champions League level," Sauer tells BBC Sport.
"But always having a core of our team coming from the Munich area and the Bavarian region with a deep identification with the club and the city.
"Our recruitment guidelines, especially for the under-11 to the under-15 teams, is trying to recruit as much talent as possible from the Munich area and the region of Bavaria."
Munich-born Croatia international Josip Stanisic is a good example. The midfielder, 26, signed as an under-17 player from local outfit SC Furstenfeldbruck, while 22-year-old Aleksandar Pavlovic joined the academy aged eight and has worked his way up to the first team and is a Germany international.
But perhaps the biggest name to come out of the academy in recent times is Jamal Musiala. The former Chelsea youth player, who joined aged 16, is a star for Bayern and Germany and has already won six Bundesliga titles at just 23 years old.
It was part of the club's strategy to bring in the best young foreign players, and those with German passports, to the club, but they also enjoyed a bit of luck.
The move came around the time Bayern Munich were interested in then-Chelsea winger Callum Hudson-Odoi, who shared the same agent as Musiala, who moved from Germany to England when he was seven.
Bayern were already aware of Musiala because he was born in Germany, but the timing was right to make a deal happen.
"There were for sure some pieces that came together at that time," Sauer says.
"I think one reason why we fought for the player at that time was the reason we had the feeling that Chelsea is not really seeing his full potential to be a top player for their first team.
"Because, otherwise, if they would have seen him as a future prospect, then it would been hard, even for Bayern Munich, to get a player out of the Chelsea environment."
Other young players in the first-team squad include 18-year-old Bara Sapoko Ndiaye, signed from Gambinos Stars Africa in The Gambia, and 18-year-old Lennart Karl, who joined the academy four years ago and has been capped by Germany.
How Bayern recruit
The Bayern Campus can house up to 43 players in accommodation, predominantly local players before they widen the search overseas.
"I think there is basically kind of a guideline that we want to have a minimum 60% of the players coming from the region and reaching the level of the under-19 age group," Sauer says.
"This automatically means that the other 40% of the team has to be recruited from other regions nationwide.
"Coming to an age group of under-17, we are also reaching out to the main European football markets to recruit the most talented players internationally.
"Jamal Musiala is one perfect example. As soon as we're coming to an age of 16 and the regulations allow us to do international transfers, we want to recruit the best talents in Europe. That's for sure part of our recruitment philosophy."
Another piece that fell into place for Musiala was the Bayern under-17 team at that time was coached by Miroslav Klose, the former Bayern forward who is the record goalscorer for Germany.
Klose is credited with pushing Musiala to work on the defensive side of his game. He also knew what a player needed to get to the highest level, with the former striker becoming an assistant to Hansi Flick when Musiala joined the first team.
That idea of having former players in charge of the next generation continues.
Ex-Bayern centre-back Dante, who also played for Nice for more than 10 years, is the current under-19 head coach.
"They can inject a little bit of the Bayern Munich DNA into the players," Sauer explains. "More from a personality side, not necessarily from a playing style.
"He also has some different ideas on the playing style but you know playing for Bayern Munich and being in the first team of Bayern Munich, at least they can tell our players what they have to be from a character, from a personality to make it up to the first team."
With so many players coming into the system and a difficult first-team set-up to break into, the Bayern style remains consistent throughout age groups.
Coaches are given guidelines to work towards but it does not stop them from having their own ideas as they aim for a style of "dominance and intensity".
"But football is always a process of evaluation," Sauer says.
"Opening the campus in 2017, we have put a very clear idea of football in place, but always kept the openness to add in ideas from coaches like [Jupp] Heynckes, [Julian] Nagelsmann, [Thomas] Tuchel, Hansi Flick, and, for sure, [current Bayern manager Vincent] Kompany. The football is always developing.
"So we have to be open enough always to amend little things. But I would say that the overall strategy is still what it was in the times of Heynckes, Pep Guardiola or Louis van Gaal."

items.text:
Colombia president says 'all hostages rescued' from supermarket siege
Colombia's President President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Wednesday that around 20 hostages being held by gunmen in a supermarket in Cartagena had been rescued. Security forces earlier entered the scene of the hours-long siege after several explosions were heard.
Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early Wednesday, successfully rescuing around 20 hostages being held by armed men, Colombia's President President Abelardo de la Espriella said.
Espriella said one hostage-taker was killed in the rescue operation which began after several explosions were heard and security forces moved into the building after an hours-long siege.
Authorities said 10 of the roughly 30 hostages initially held had been released after hours of negotiations, including several elderly women.
Gunmen earlier seized dozens of hostages at a supermarket in Cartagena on Tuesday, triggering a tense standoff with police, troops and special forces who surrounded the building and cut power to the area.
Authorities said the gunmen had attempted to rob an armoured vehicle before fleeing into the supermarket and taking about 30 people hostage as police closed in.
Reuters images showed heavily armed military and police gathered outside the supermarket.
President Abelardo de la Espriella travelled to Cartagena as the crisis unfolded and met security commanders at the scene to ostensibly take control of a massive operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.
"Thirty people were kidnapped, five of whom have already been released. They are ‌older women," De la Espriella had said earlier from the city of Villavicencio, where he traveled following an overnight ‌bombing there.
"All the capabilities of our various security forces, have now been deployed, including special units," he added.
Read moreA president among body bags: Photo ops spark outrage in Colombia
The Rafael Núñez airport in Cartagena briefly suspended landings as the armed forces used one of the runways in connection with the incident. Landings were reopened about 45 minutes after the suspension.
Local media reported the hostages are being at the Castellana location of the Exito supermarket chain.
Images on social media showed some people kneeling against the windows of the store earlier on Tuesday, their hands seemingly bound. Reuters could not immediately independently verify the images.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

Muhammad Zeeshan
items.text:
Pakistan rejoices as country’s first astronaut enters orbit
Zeeshan Ali makes history as the first foreign national to board China’s space station
The first person from Pakistan to go into orbit has made history as the first foreign astronaut to board China’s Tiangong space station.
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali docked at the space station in the early hours of Wednesday after taking off from China’s Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China on board a Chinese-made rocket.
Ali, 40, will stay in space for five to 10 days, shorter than the usual six-month stints Chinese astronauts serve.
“I’m not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder,” Ali told reporters on Tuesday.
While most of the infrastructure behind Ali’s space trip is Chinese, he has trained for months in China, including by learning Chinese, to make the trip happen.
“This is not just one astronaut’s journey, but the journey of 240 million Pakistanis. It is the journey of our younger generation, our scientists and our dreams,” Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said in a post on X.
“This is living proof of the ironclad friendship between Pakistan and China. We are grateful to our brother country, China, for making Pakistan part of this historic mission.”
Chinese President Xi Jinping said the joint mission with astronauts from China and Pakistan is “a vivid embodiment of the deep-rooted friendship between the two countries”.
This is a big diplomatic moment for China. Beijing is eager to show the world that the Tiangong space station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
China has been ramping up its space industry and aims to put a Chinese astronaut on the moon by 2030. The US aims to do the same in 2028, for the first time since the 1972 Apollo 17 flight.
China plans to establish a ‌research ‌base on the moon by 2035 with Russia.
Both Beijing and Washington insist their presence in space is entirely peaceful, but the US has warned that China could seek to dominate resource-rich areas of the moon.

items.title: Villeneuve: Verstappen showed 'race craft' edge over Mercedes pair in Vegas
items.summary:
Max Verstappen showed 'race craft' edge over George Russell and Kimi Antonelli during Las Vegas GP, says Jacques Villeneuve
Max Verstappen withstood pressure from Mercedes' George Russell and Kimi Antonelli on his way to winning a thrilling Las Vegas GP for Red Bull; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live
items.text:
Max Verstappen showed 'race craft' edge over George Russell and Kimi Antonelli during Las Vegas GP, says Jacques Villeneuve
Max Verstappen withstood pressure from Mercedes' George Russell and Kimi Antonelli on his way to winning a thrilling Las Vegas GP for Red Bull; watch the Qatar Grand Prix live on Sky Sports this weekend, with qualifying at 6pm on Saturday and the race at 4pm on Sunday
Tuesday 24 November 2026 21:25, UK
Former Formula 1 world champion Jacques Villeneuve says Max Verstappen's Las Vegas Grand Prix victory showed that Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell will not be able to beat the Red Bull driver in next year's championship unless they have a superior car.
Verstappen retained the lead from pole position at the start but was challenged by Russell and then later Antonelli for almost the entire 50-lap race amid near constant changes of position throughout the field, but the Red Bull driver expertly saw off their best efforts before both made late errors to drop down the order.
Antonelli has already been crowned 2026 world champion after Mercedes' dominance early in the season helped him build a significant advantage, but Verstappen is putting together an ominous finish to the year, with the four-time world champion having won four of the last six races and claimed nine successive podiums.
- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column
- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Sky Sports F1 pundit and 1997 F1 world champion Villeneuve said after the race: "It was exciting. People will say there was a battery involved [in all the passes], but it doesn't matter.
"We saw some race craft. Max was above and the two Mercedes drivers were lacking in that respect.
"And what it is telling us is that unless next year Mercedes have a car that's superior, they can't win because there's something missing."
A combination of factors, most notably the extreme power of the slipstream effect, meant there were more than 350 overtakes during a breathless race at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit.
The lead changed hands 34 times, but every time Verstappen was overtaken, which on almost every occasion was by a Mercedes, the four-time world champion retook his position within a few corners.
Russell locked up and hit a barrier as he tried to pass Antonelli for second in the closing stages, before the Italian suffered a loss of power at the start of the final lap after incorrectly lifting off the throttle as he was preparing to mount a final challenge to Verstappen.
Villeneuve was also impressed by the drives of seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton and last year's title winner Lando Norris, who took advantage of the Mercedes errors to finish second ahead of his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri.
Hamilton could have also ended up on the podium had it not been for him spinning in a contentious collision with his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.
"You could see that Lewis had good race craft as well as Lando," Villeneuve added.
"It was really fun to see. We saw today a race where you don't need pit stops, you don't need tyres that degrade.
"We had a race where drivers could push like qualifying laps all the time and that allowed them to race. It was great fun."

items.text:
Bangladesh garment workers win 36% pay rise after weeks of protest
The protests have cost Bangladesh hundreds of millions, but it is unclear whether workers will accept the offer.
Workers in Bangladesh’s garment sector have been offered a 36 percent pay rise after months of protests that are estimated to have cost the country’s economy hundreds of millions of dollars.
The chairman of Bangladesh’s government-appointed garment industry wage board said on Wednesday that the “majority” of the board had agreed to increase the sector’s minimum wage from 12,500 taka ($100) to 17,500 taka ($136) monthly.
Bangladesh’s central bank calls the garment sector the “country’s export engine”. It earns roughly $38bn a year, employs four million people, and accounts for four-fifths of the country’s exports. Many of the industry’s workers are women in rural areas.
The 17,500 taka offered is below the 30,000 taka ($240) that protesters had asked for, and it’s not currently clear whether they will accept the amount offered.
“Although we are not completely satisfied, the outcome is not entirely bad either,” Babul Akhter, the labour representative on a wage board set up to resolve the crisis, told reporters. Akhter urged workers to return to their factories.
“Previously, workers used to get a wage revision every five years, but this time they are getting a revised wage after three years.”
The wage hike will take effect in December, with workers receiving the new salaries in January.
An economic success
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) said on Sunday that protests had cost the industry an estimated $428m in losses, while orders worth $254m had moved to other countries.
Bangladesh is the world’s second-largest garment exporter, behind China. Home to 170 million people, the garment industry has proved an economic success story that has driven development in the South Asian country.
That has, at times, come at a cost: in 2013, the Rana Plaza factory collapse killed 1,134 people and injured thousands, exposing poor safety standards and working conditions for the millions of workers in the industry.
Numerous other incidents, including fires, have resulted in deaths – sometimes killing dozens.

items.text:
Domestic violence soars to record high in Germany
November 25, 2026
The German government has presented some grim statistics with regard to misogyny, rape, violence and murder, with reported cases of domestic violence at an all-time high.
At a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig released the latest figures on crimes that specifically target women: whether within families and intimate relationships, in public or online.
'Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories'
In contrast to the statistics pertaining to crime overall, which have remained the same or increased only slightly, reports of crimes against women have increased.
"Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories, people and particularly women and girls, whose lives are severely affected by these acts of violence," said Dobrindt.
In 2025, some 280,000 people were victims of physical abuse in their own homes, a 2.8% increase compared to the previous year. Over 70% of the victims were female. Each hour, 16 women are subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors.
The male victims included boys who had been assaulted by their fathers.
The number of misogynistic hate crimes has also risen dramatically, by almost 50%, to 819 cases.
"The figures show us what it can mean to be a woman in Germany," said Hubig. "It can mean being killed by one's partner or ex-partner. Being a woman can also mean being physically abused by one's partner or ex-partner in one's own home. Being a woman can mean that one's sexual autonomy is brutally disregarded."
Perpetrators, victims getting younger
According to the latest findings, both perpetrators and victims are getting younger. In 2025, nearly half of all female victims of sexual offenses were under the age of 18. And the number of incidents of online violence against women and girls rose by 15.7%. This includes the unauthorized sharing of videos and photos, verbal abuse, manipulation of images, threats and online blackmail, as well as cyberstalking.
Because many perpetrators and victims are still in their teens, Prien, who is also minister for education, said the government wanted to focus primarily on schools, which she explained should become places of prevention.
"Ultimately, we need to bring about a change in people's mindsets, especially those of men. That will be the deciding factor in the end," she said.
Femicides to be classified as murder, not manslaughter
Over the weekend, Justice Minister Hubig had already announced that in future all femicides, the intentional killing of girls and women because of their gender, would be classified as murders. Currently, such crimes are often classified as manslaughter, for which the penalty is less severe than for murder.
Hubig told German broadcaster ZDF that it was increasingly common that femicides be described as family tragedies or as domestic dramas revolving around jealousy and then classified as manslaughter.
Martina Link, the vice president of the Federal Criminal Police Office, was also at the press conference in Berlin. She called for everybody to pay closer attention to the issue, within their own families, neighborhoods or at work.
"Violence against women is not a private matter," she said. "Not in our immediate surroundings nor in the digital world."
She also pointed out that when it came to sexual offenses and domestic violence, only about 5-10% of cases were reported.
This article was originally written in German.

items.title: TSC to hire 20,000 teachers, convert 24,000 interns to permanent jobs
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) plans to recruit an additional 24,000 teachers in the 2027/28 financial year as the government steps up efforts to address the persistent teacher shortage in public schools.
TSC Chief Executive Officer Cheptumo Ayabei told the National A
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – The Teachers Service Commission (TSC) plans to recruit an additional 24,000 teachers in the 2027/28 financial year as the government steps up efforts to address the persistent teacher shortage in public schools.
TSC Chief Executive Officer Cheptumo Ayabei told the National Assembly Education Committee that the recruitment forms part of the commission’s performance targets for the financial year, as it seeks to bridge staffing gaps across the country’s basic education institutions.
Appearing before the committee, chaired by Julius Melly, during consideration of the 2026/27 Budget Policy Statement, Ayabei said the commission had recruited more than 100,000 teachers over the previous three financial years as part of the government’s Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA).
The government had set a target of recruiting 116,000 teachers to reduce the shortage in public schools, with the commission planning to recruit a further 20,000 in the 2026/27 financial year to meet that target.
“The Commission plans to recruit a further 20,000 teachers in FY 2026/2027 to achieve the BETA target of 116,000. Further, TSC shall convert 24,000 teacher interns to permanent and pensionable terms in FY 2027/28 as a strategy to continuously address the existing teacher shortage,” Ayabei told the committee.
The planned recruitment will come alongside the conversion of 24,000 teacher interns to permanent and pensionable terms in 2027/28, a move intended to improve job security for teachers who have been serving on internship contracts while addressing staffing needs.
The two measures form part of the government’s broader efforts to improve teacher availability as schools continue to grapple with uneven distribution of staff, increased enrolment and the demands of the Competency-Based Education (CBE) curriculum.
Teacher shortages have been particularly challenging in some rural, marginalised and hard-to-staff areas, where schools struggle to attract and retain teachers across different subject specialisations.
The staffing pressure has also been compounded by the transition to the new education structure, which requires additional teachers, particularly as learners progress through junior and senior school.
Funding gap
Meanwhile, the State Department for Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) has proposed a budget of Sh84.129 billion for the 2027/28 financial year against an allocation ceiling of Sh64.767 billion, leaving a funding gap of approximately Sh19.4 billion.
Principal Secretary Esther Muoria told the committee that the shortfall could affect the department’s ability to implement key programmes, including scholarships, grants and the construction of additional TVET institutions.
She said the department remained committed to developing middle-level technical skills needed to support economic growth and improve Kenya’s competitiveness in the global economy.
“We have presented a total resource requirement of Kshs.84.129 billion for FY 2027/28, against a ceiling of Kshs.64.767 billion, leaving a deficit of Kshs.19.425 billion. The underfunded priorities include scholarships, grants, and construction of TVET institutions,” Muoria said.
She added that strengthening technical and vocational training was essential in promoting entrepreneurship, investment, productivity and employment opportunities.
Capitation shortfalls
The State Department for Basic Education has also proposed a budget of Sh140.18 billion for the 2027/28 financial year, up from the Sh136.55 billion approved for 2026/27.
The proposed allocation comprises Sh121.93 billion for recurrent expenditure and Sh18.24 billion for development programmes.
However, the department faces significant funding gaps in key areas, particularly free primary education and junior school capitation.
According to Principal Secretary John Ololtuaa, free primary education has been allocated Sh7.01 billion against a requirement of Sh9.97 billion, leaving a shortfall of approximately Sh2.96 billion.
The allocation is intended to support capitation for 6.39 million learners, with the department also providing for additional funding for learners with special educational needs in integrated schools and special needs boarding institutions.
The funding shortfall is more pronounced in junior school, where the department has proposed Sh30.72 billion against a requirement of Sh54.23 billion, leaving a deficit of Sh23.51 billion.
Ololtuaa said the requirement was based on regular capitation for 3.58 million learners at Sh15,043 per learner.
The funding gaps raise concerns over the adequacy of resources available to schools as the government continues implementing the Competency-Based Education curriculum, which requires additional learning materials, infrastructure and specialised teaching support.
The State Department for Higher Education and Research and the State Department for Science, Research and Innovation also appeared before the committee to present their budget proposals and funding priorities for the 2027/28 financial year.

More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.
Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for
items.text:
Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.
Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.
Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.
The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.
Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."
Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.
"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."
Morocco raises concerns over CAS process
Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.
In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.
The CAS director general, Matthieu Reeb, acknowledged to reporters at the court in Lausanne that a Moroccan protest was received just minutes before the verdict was announced.
Reeb said the court's panel "in charge of petitions for challenge has conceded that there was not enough elements at this stage to postpone the notification of the award."
CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds of which a judge's integrity could be one.
Haas has been among the most respected and in-demand CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected by parties in storied cases involving Manchester City's beating a Champions League ban by UEFA, tennis star Simona Halep's doping case and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.
Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal."
Trouble on the field and in the stands
Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.
The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).
Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.
Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz — a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka" — was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.
The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognized as the champion at that point.
Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.
Soccer's laws versus regulations
Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.
The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally can't be taken to the sports court.
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met — both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.
In the first legal case in March, CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."
The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.
The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.
Soccer fans in Senegal celebrate a win
"Senegal won on the pitch, and the court simply confirmed what we all already knew: We are the real champions of Africa," said Mariama Sidibé, 35, an accountant in the capital, Dakar.
Sidibé said the dispute between Morocco and Senegal should now be left in the past.
"With all of this behind us, we should focus on what unites us now, and who knows, maybe Morocco can have its revenge on the field during the next AFCON this summer," she said.
"At the end of the day Morocco and Senegal are brothers," Sidibé added, referring to the countries' long shared clos

In 2022, an indepe
items.text:
Court to rule on South African president's bid to set aside 'Farmgate' report
- Published
A South African court is due to rule on President Cyril Ramaphosa's attempt to overturn a report that found he has a case to answer over the theft of large sums of cash from his private farm.
In 2022, an independent panel said Ramaphosa may have committed serious misconduct relating to the theft of $580,000 (£443,000), hidden in a sofa, at his Phala Phala game farm in the Limpopo province. He denied any wrongdoing.
Ramaphosa challenged the findings of the report after the Constitutional Court ruled that parliament had violated the constitution by blocking moves to impeach him.
The ruling could either exonerate the president or clear the way for him to possibly face impeachment.
Wednesday's ruling will be handed down by the Western Cape high court - the same court that blocked a parliamentary committee from proceeding with the impeachment process while a review challenge of the report is under way.
The scandal, dubbed "Farmgate" by local media, has has dogged Ramaphosa since it emerged in 2022, when former spy chief Arthur Fraser reported the matter to police in a dossier.
Fraser, an ally of former President Jacob Zuma, accused Ramaphosa of concealing the theft from the police and tax authorities.
The break-in happened in 2020, when thieves allegedly stole bundles of US dollar bills hidden inside a sofa at the farm.
Earlier this month, two people were found guilty of the theft.
Ramaphosa confirmed that a robbery had taken place but said the money had been from the legitimate sale of buffalo from his livestock business.
Several investigations cleared him of any wrongdoing, but parliament began an impeachment proceedings in 2022 and appointed an independent panel to investigate the allegations.
The panel made a series of damaging findings, including that there was "substantial doubt about the legitimacy of the source of the currency that was stolen".
It also concluded that Ramaphosa "has a case to answer".
Ramaphosa initially challenged the report in court but withdrew his application after parliament voted against adopting its findings.
He revived the legal challenge again in May this year after the Constitutional Court, the country's highest court, ruled that parliament had acted unconstitutionally by blocking moves to impeach him.
It ordered parliament to refer the report to an impeachment committee.
In his latest challenge, Ramaphosa argued that the panel had "misconceived its mandate, misjudged the information placed before it and misinterpreted the four charges advanced against me".
If the Western Cape High Court rules in his favour, it could bring the current impeachment process to an end, unless parliament successfully challenges the decision.
A ruling against him would allow the parliamentary committee to examine the charges against the president and make a recommendation.
If the committee recommends impeachment, parliament would have to vote on whether to remove him from office. This would require the support of at least two-thirds majority in parliament.
Ramaphosa's Africa National Congress (ANC) has enough parliamentary seats to block such a move.
He is the first president to face impeachment proceedings under the rules introduced in 2018.

items.text:
Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?
- Published
Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'big six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.
Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it begs the question: are United this season's Spurs?
Well while Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points, they actually started the season better than United have. After 11 games last season, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.
But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.
While the table was prompting talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.
United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.
But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.
While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.
Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.
But what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement quickly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.
And it's not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.
As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.
By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the % chance of each club finishing in each position in the League.
While the above means it's more likely United will survive, it's worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.
There's a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.
History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.
Of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.
A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has ever finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.
Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.
Having said that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there wouldn't be entirely unprecedented.
It's a big ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they've played than they did last season.
Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last season
Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.
While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams currently in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals
So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, Pochettino will hope to quickly quash any concerns his new club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

items.summary:
UK sent sex offender refugee to African country in undisclosed deal

The UK forcibly resettled a refugee and convicted sex offender in an African country with which he had no connection, in a deal not disclosed to the UK Parliament or the local community.
The man, who was from Sri Lanka a
items.text:
UK sent sex offender refugee to African country in undisclosed deal
- Published
The UK forcibly resettled a refugee and convicted sex offender in an African country with which he had no connection, in a deal not disclosed to the UK Parliament or the local community.
The man, who was from Sri Lanka and had a history of severe mental illness and suicide attempts, took his own life months after arriving in Eswatini.
The BBC has obtained a copy of the draft deal between the two governments, in which the UK pledges to cover the costs of his resettlement for up to three years.
The UK government was finalising plans for 35-year-old Kishanth Peramalya to live there permanently when he died.
Migration experts told the BBC this was the first known case of the UK government forcibly resettling in such a manner a refugee permanently overseas.
In 2024, the Labour government scrapped a controversial plan to send asylum seekers with pending claims to Rwanda. Now it wants to send failed asylum seekers overseas to third countries when they cannot be sent to their home countries, but is yet to announce any deals. Last week, five EU countries reached a deal to send people whose claims have been refused to Rwanda.
The Eswatini deal raises questions about how much the UK government should disclose about such arrangements, and how it protects both the people it sends overseas and the communities that receive them.
The UK government told the BBC that protecting the British public was its priority and that it "continue[s] to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case".
Peramalya's family is demanding answers about his treatment, while critics in Eswatini have accused Britain of using their country as a "dumping ground".
Royal Navy rescue
In 2021, the Royal Navy rescued Peramalya in the Indian Ocean, along with dozens of other Sri Lankan asylum seekers, as they tried to sail from India to Canada.
They were then detained in a camp on Diego Garcia, an island in the British Indian Ocean Territory, run exclusively as a UK-US military base.
The island's authorities, who answer to London, recognised that Peramalya and others could not safely return to Sri Lanka, and awarded them refugee protections. But the group remained in the camp for three years while British officials debated their future. A court later ruled their detention had been unlawful.
As a teenager, Peramalya had been tortured and sexually abused by officers in the Sri Lankan military and was later diagnosed with PTSD. During his detention on Diego Garcia, his mental health deteriorated, according to court papers. He suffered from depression and anxiety, and repeatedly attempted suicide. UN inspectors who came to the island raised concerns over the conditions he was being kept in.
While there, he committed a series of crimes, including assault and arson, during two suicide attempts, and spent 24 weeks in prison. He was also convicted of four counts of sexual assault for which he received a suspended prison sentence.
In December 2024, most of the Sri Lankan asylum seekers were allowed to enter the UK but ministers refused to let Peramalya join them because of his crimes. He remained on Diego Garcia.
The High Court upheld the UK's refusal to admit him, in part because of the risk he posed and because ministers were making genuine efforts to find somewhere else safe for him to live. Court documents, seen by the BBC, show the UK approached more than 20 countries and could not secure an agreement.
Undisclosed British deal
Then, in February 2026, the US began using its military base on Diego Garcia in its war with Iran. The island authorities began withdrawing non-essential personnel.
At the end of March, the Maldives offered to take Peramalya for 30 days. He was transferred there before being sent on to Eswatini, formerly known as Swaziland.
At the time of his death, the British and Eswatini governments had been finalising the agreement for Peramalya to live there permanently, with the UK to pay for the "reasonable costs" of his accommodation, healthcare, and other support for up to three years.
The document does not specify a total cost or explain how the two governments would manage the risks Peramalya posed to himself and others. But it explicitly acknowledged he required support that would meet his basic needs and protect his physical and mental health, and wellbeing.
Peramalya's family has told the BBC he was initially placed in an isolated guesthouse on his own.
Speaking from India, his sister said the family had not been aware of the plan to make his transfer permanent, and that his mental health had worsened while in the country.
She said he would call her four times a day. "My brother did not want to go there at all," she said. "He couldn't manage being there alone, he was very lonely." The family also said it had been unaware of sexual offences committed by him.
He initially saw a psychiatrist weekly, she said. Later, after his mental health declined, he had daily appointments, and an attendant was brought in to prepare his food.
On 13 September, he took his own life.
The UN's refugee agency, which had previously raised concerns about Peramalya's condition on Diego Garcia, said it was "deeply saddened" by his death and stressed that refugees being transferred to other different countries must be protected.
"UNHCR recognises that asylum seekers and refugees may, in certain circumstances, be lawfully transferred to a third country. However, this requires that specific safeguards are in place and those conditions are fulfilled in practice."
'Highly unusual' arrangement
Peter Walsh, of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, described the case as "highly unusual".
"In most cases, people with criminal convictions who cannot be returned to their home country would simply remain in the UK. Third countries are generally quite reluctant to accept foreign national offenders," he said.

items.summary:
Four years after huge asteroid crash, a spacecraft has now returned to assess the damage
- Published
A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.
It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately sma
items.text:
Four years after huge asteroid crash, a spacecraft has now returned to assess the damage
- Published
A spacecraft has arrived at an asteroid to investigate the damage caused by an unprecedented cosmic crash.
It what may sound like the plot of a disaster movie, Nasa's Dart spacecraft deliberately smashed into the space rock in 2022 to knock it off course.
The Nasa craft was obliterated on impact. Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) mission, called Hera, is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision - with the first images set to be released later on Wednesday.
The asteroid poses no threat, instead this was the first ever test of our planetary defences to see what action we could take if a space rock was heading for our planet.
"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.
The crash test focussed on a pair of asteroids: a larger one called Didymos - about 730m (2,400ft) wide - which is orbited by a smaller rock called Dimorphos, about 150m (490ft) wide.
The Dart spacecraft targeted Dimorphos, hurtling into the rock at 22,000km per hour (14,000mph). Images beamed back showed the asteroid's rocky surface coming ever closer until the feed cut out on impact.
It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 10,000km long (6,200 miles), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.
The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.
Before the collision it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the Dart crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.
But the arrival of the second spacecraft, Hera, will help scientists to answer many more questions.
"Dart exploded in the asteroid, and therefore we don't have the information of what is its final state," explained Michel.
"The impact could have left a crater - and if it is the case, we need to understand the size and the depth. Or [the impact] may have entirely reshaped the asteroid."
The Hera mission will spend the next year studying Dimorphos, and take a look at Didymos too.
The spacecraft is packed with instruments, and it also has two small shoe-boxed sized satellites onboard, which can study the impact site up close, and then later land on the asteroid.
A key task is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.
This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.
"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.
"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."
Asteroids pose a significant threat to our planet.
The biggest, which measure more than a kilometre across, could cause global devastation. But medium-sized asteroids around the same dimensions as Dimorphos could wipe out a city.
"We all know what happened to the dinosaurs, right? And we don't want that to happen to us," said Carolyn Ernst, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, who works on both the Dart and Hera missions.
"The good news for us is that there are far fewer potential threats out there in the Solar System than there were millions of years ago. But there are objects out there."
She said the biggest asteroids have been spotted, and none are heading to Earth.
"The smallest stuff isn't too much of a threat because our atmosphere protects us," she added.
"But there's a size range in the middle where we don't know where all of them are, and it could, if impacted, cause problems for humanity. And if we can find out about that and know about that, well, we sure as heck would want to try to stop that."
Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks - to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.
A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids: a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.
There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.
Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.
But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.
This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.
Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

items.title: Hysa aims to win WBC title then take on 'favourite fighter' Fury
items.summary:
Nelson Hysa aims to beat Agit Kabayel, win WBC world title and take on Tyson Fury, his 'favourite fighter'
Nelson Hysa challenges Agit Kabayel for the WBC title on Saturday in Dusseldorf; Hard-punching Hysa hopes to upset popular German Kabayel and then look to take on his 'favourite fighter' Tyson
items.text:
Nelson Hysa aims to beat Agit Kabayel, win WBC world title and take on Tyson Fury, his 'favourite fighter'
Nelson Hysa challenges Agit Kabayel for the WBC title on Saturday in Dusseldorf; Hard-punching Hysa hopes to upset popular German Kabayel and then look to take on his 'favourite fighter' Tyson Fury; Hysa says Moses Itauma is still the best in the division - 'I don't want to fight him!'
Tuesday 24 November 2026 19:23, UK
Nelson Hysa has a vision. He wants to dethrone Agit Kabayel, win the WBC heavyweight world title and then take on his favourite fighter – Tyson Fury.
Hysa, unbeaten in 25 professional fights, challenges Kabayel on Saturday for the WBC heavyweight world championship.
The Albanian has taken 23 of those wins inside the distance and is looking to upset the popular German when they fight in Dusseldorf this weekend.
A power-puncher, Hysa told Sky Sports: "The knockout was with me from the first day that I started boxing.
"In this match [against Kabayel] I am preparing to do more good rounds because I know the opponent is a very good boxer, he's a tough boxer, a serious boxer.
"But we are planning, we are trying to do our best. We have our strategy to win the match and I think we will win the match earlier than the 12th round.
"I need to move up the ratio of knockouts!"
With Oleksandr Usyk vacating his championships, there are now new belt-holders in the division, but Hysa does not consider Kabayel the best of the current heavyweight titlists.
"For me No 1 now of the guys that have the belts, No 1 is Filip Hrgovic, [then Daniel] Dubois and for me the special one is Tyson Fury.
"Hrgovic will do very good because he's a good boxer," Hysa added. "Hrgovic beat the best guy in the heavyweight division. He beat Moses [Itauma]. I don't want to do a fight with Moses, he's a good guy! He will be the best heavyweight in the world. He is the best heavyweight in the world but he needs more time."
Fury will fight Anthony Joshua for the WBA 'super' heavyweight title when they meet on December 11. Hysa tips Fury to win and is eager to box him in a unification if he comes through his own fight.
"Who doesn't want to fight Tyson Fury? He's a legend," Hysa said. "The No 1 man at heavyweight.
"He's my No 1 favourite boxer, I love him, I love everything he does. His style, everything.
"Who doesn't want to fight Tyson Fury?"

items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – Nairobi City County Government is stepping up efforts to combat gender-based violence (GBV) through a citywide campaign targeting communities, schools and neighbourhoods across the capital.
The county will officially launch the 2026 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based V
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – Nairobi City County Government is stepping up efforts to combat gender-based violence (GBV) through a citywide campaign targeting communities, schools and neighbourhoods across the capital.
The county will officially launch the 2026 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence campaign at Eastleigh High School, bringing together government agencies, development partners, civil society organisations and local communities.
The campaign, coordinated through the Sub-Sector of Gender and Inclusivity, seeks to strengthen advocacy, community engagement and coordinated action to prevent and respond to all forms of gender-based violence.
County Executive Committee Member for Inclusivity Rosemary Kariuki said the initiative was aimed at building safer neighbourhoods, schools, workplaces and homes while ensuring survivors can access support and protection.
Kariuki noted that Nairobi’s rapid urban growth and socio-economic pressures could increase vulnerability to domestic and gender-based violence, requiring stronger collaboration between government agencies and communities.
She said the county, under Governor Johnson Sakaja’s administration, was prioritising awareness, survivor protection and the promotion of human rights and dignity.
“Ending gender-based violence requires a united front where the County Government, national agencies, development partners and our communities walk hand in hand,” Kariuki said.
Chief Officer for Inclusivity Dr Irene Muchoki said the campaign would focus on strengthening survivor-centred support systems and prevention mechanisms across all 17 sub-counties.
She said the county was working to improve survivors’ access to justice, healthcare and psychosocial support services while ensuring that protection mechanisms were accessible at the grassroots level.
Director for Gender Jane Gichure highlighted the importance of involving young people and local communities in challenging harmful practices and promoting gender equality.
Gichure said hosting the launch at Eastleigh High School underscored the importance of engaging students and the wider community in efforts to confront gender-based violence.
She urged Nairobi residents to break the silence surrounding abuse and actively support efforts to establish a culture of respect, accountability and zero tolerance for violence.
During the 16-day campaign, the county’s Gender and Inclusivity Sub-Sector will roll out targeted awareness activities and community dialogues aimed at connecting residents with protection and support services.
The initiative will bring together county officials, partner organisations and community leaders to strengthen collective efforts towards eliminating gender-based violence and building a safer, more inclusive Nairobi.

items.title: Nairobi Residents Invited to Shape 2027/28 County Budget in Two-Day Public Forums
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – Nairobi City County Government has launched a two-day public participation exercise across all 17 sub-counties to gather residents’ views on the draft 2027 County Fiscal Strategy Paper (CFSP).
The exercise, which began on Wednesday will conclude on Thursday, providing reside
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – Nairobi City County Government has launched a two-day public participation exercise across all 17 sub-counties to gather residents’ views on the draft 2027 County Fiscal Strategy Paper (CFSP).
The exercise, which began on Wednesday will conclude on Thursday, providing residents, businesses and other stakeholders an opportunity to influence spending priorities for the 2027/2028 financial year.
The programme is being spearheaded by County Director of Economic Planning Geoffrey Sianga and is anchored in Section 117 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012, and Article 10 of the Constitution.
County Executive Committee Member for Finance and Economic Affairs Ibrahim Auma said the CFSP provides the fiscal framework that will guide the county’s budget and medium-term priorities.
He noted that the document will determine resource allocation to key services, including road infrastructure, healthcare, waste management and water supply, while also informing local business levies and land rates.
“The CFSP dictates where every shilling goes in the next financial year. We want a budget built around the real needs of Nairobians,” Auma said.
He urged residents, business owners and community leaders across the county to attend the forums, scrutinise the proposals and submit recommendations on how resources should be prioritised.
County Chief Officer for Economic Planning John Lintari said public participation was critical in strengthening evidence-based planning and aligning the county’s fiscal priorities with its development objectives.
He said feedback from residents and stakeholders would help the county identify emerging needs, assess competing demands and allocate resources more effectively to support inclusive and sustainable development.
Geoffrey Sianga, an economist in the Finance Sector, said technical teams would be deployed across all 17 sub-counties to explain the proposed fiscal allocations and collect views from residents and special interest groups.
The teams will also guide participants through the county’s economic outlook and proposed sector spending ceilings to ensure grassroots recommendations inform the final policy document.
The county has invited residents, neighbourhood associations, civil society organisations and private sector representatives to participate in the exercise.
Those unable to attend the physical forums can access the draft 2027 CFSP through the county website, www.nairobi.go.ke, and submit written memoranda by Thursday, November 26.
Submissions can be sent via email to [email protected] or delivered physically to the Public Participation Offices on the second floor of the Main City Hall.
The public participation process is intended to ensure Nairobi residents have a direct role in shaping county spending priorities before the budget ceilings are finalised.

items.title: Govt Assures eCitizen Platform Remains Operational Amid Data Access Probe
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – The government has assured Kenyans that the eCitizen platform remains fully operational as it investigates reports of unauthorised access to data held on the digital services portal.
The State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services stated that its technical and secu
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 25 – The government has assured Kenyans that the eCitizen platform remains fully operational as it investigates reports of unauthorised access to data held on the digital services portal.
The State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services stated that its technical and security teams are working with relevant government agencies to establish the extent of the reported incident.
In a statement, the department said it was treating the reports seriously but maintained that “members of the public could continue accessing government services through the platform as investigations proceed.”
The government has, however, urged eCitizen users to remain vigilant against possible fraudsters seeking to exploit the reports through fraudulent calls, text messages, emails and suspicious links.
Users have been cautioned against sharing their passwords or one-time PINs (OTPs), with the department emphasising that eCitizen will never request such credentials.
Kenyans who use the same password across different platforms have also been advised to change their eCitizen credentials and adopt strong, unique passwords.
The public has further been encouraged to report any suspicious activity on their accounts.
The department said it would issue further updates through official communication channels as investigations progress, urging the public and media to avoid circulating unverified information.
Protecting personal data held by government systems remains a priority, the department said, without disclosing the extent of the reported unauthorised access.

items.title: Phone spying to missiles: Why India-Israel strategic ties go beyond Modi
items.summary:
Phone spying to missiles: Why India-Israel strategic ties go beyond Modi
The opposition Congress party calls Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide, but its leader still wants strong ties with Israel.
New Delhi, India – For the past three years, India’s main opposition party, the Indian National Congress,
items.text:
Phone spying to missiles: Why India-Israel strategic ties go beyond Modi
The opposition Congress party calls Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide, but its leader still wants strong ties with Israel.
New Delhi, India – For the past three years, India’s main opposition party, the Indian National Congress, has frequently criticised Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government for its refusal to condemn Israel’s war on Gaza, acknowledging it as a genocide.
Yet when asked about his position on Israel in an interview last week, the party’s de facto leader, Rahul Gandhi, was more nuanced. He condemned Israel’s genocidal war but added: “I support a strong relationship with Israel. We have strategic interests, including buying the best weapons for our armed forces.”
Those comments sparked a backlash from some of the Congress party’s allies, including left parties. But analysts said they reflect the depth of a strategic partnership that, while controversial, is seen as critical by both India and Israel. It’s a relationship that has grown dramatically under Modi but extends beyond his Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP)-led government and is one that is likely to outlast its rule.
From weapons and surveillance to policing and hacking, India has increasingly turned to Israel as a vital partner and source of expertise, binding the two countries in ways that are hard to disentangle even if the political winds shift in either nation.
This month, an investigation by the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), a nonprofit, found that Home Minister Amit Shah had waived India’s own rules to allow the purchase of phone-hacking technology from Israel.
Indians have been here before. In 2019, WhatsApp disclosed that Pegasus spyware, developed by Israel’s NSO Group, had been used to target Indian journalists and human rights defenders. Amnesty International later confirmed infections on the phones of journalists Siddharth Varadarajan and Anand Mangnale. The government denied unauthorised surveillance.
Together, the cases point to a dependency, analysts said. India’s cooperation with Israel “has always involved examining and exploring Israeli methods for intelligence gathering, border management and controlling dissent”, researcher and author Azad Essa told Al Jazeera.
“It was only a matter of time before Israeli products or methods would be used against Indians themselves, including farmers,” added Essa, author of Hostile Homelands, a book on the burgeoning alliance between India and Israel.
In Haryana, Delhi’s neighbouring state, the government there spent six years trying to replicate Israeli police and army tactics, and in February 2024, state police used drones to fire tear gas at farmers marching towards Delhi.
Far beyond surveillance
The phone tools are the newest layer of a relationship that runs deep into India’s defence industry. Since 2014, India has become Israel’s most reliable arms buyer, taking about 37 percent of its exports.
At the centre of this relationship sits the Adani Group, led by billionaire Gautam Adani, widely seen as a close Modi associate. In 2016, the Indian conglomerate formed a joint venture with Israel’s Elbit Systems to make Hermes 900 drones in Hyderabad, the first such facility outside Israel. Since 2020, Adani has held a 51 percent stake in BLR Systems, which makes Negev machinegun parts with Israel Weapon Industries. In January 2023, Adani and Israel’s Gadot completed the $1.15bn purchase of Haifa’s port, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attended the handover.
Essa says India “is increasingly becoming a manufacturing and supply base for Israeli companies”.
Ashutosh Singh, an independent researcher in New Delhi who studies Palestine and the Middle East, agreed, calling Hyderabad the best example of Indian capital embedded in Israel’s military infrastructure built “in the garb” of the Make in India initiative, a programme meant to indigenise manufacturing.
Nicolas Blarel, an associate professor of international relations at Leiden University in the Netherlands, added a note of caution. What happens in Hyderabad is “mostly late assembly” of Israeli-designed drones, he told Al Jazeera, and it is “not clear how much technology has been actually completely shared”. But he noted that deliveries were made to Israel in late 2023 and early 2024 when some of those drone models were being used for the genocide in Gaza.
Amnesty International’s “Made in India” report, published on July 30, documented 2,596 shipments of weapons, ammunition and military components from Indian firms to Israel from October 7, 2023, to November 30, 2025, referring to a period that began with the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel that served as the trigger for the assault on Gaza.
It named nine companies, three of them wholly owned by India’s Ministry of Defence, and concluded that the Indian state itself was transferring weapons whenever those firms export. Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the next day that India had a “robust” legal framework for strategic trade without addressing the allegations.
Why India buys: No strings attached
Ask analysts why India keeps buying from Israel, and the answer is less about technology than about what Israel does not demand in return.
Kabir Taneja of the Observer Research Foundation think tank said defence carries almost the entire relationship. A country that sells India a Western platform may refuse to share the source code needed to fit an Indian-built missile on it. Israel has been willing to bridge those gaps, for instance by fitting early-warning radars to a Russian Il-76 aircraft.
“Israel is that Walmart of defence technologies that you can just go and purchase without any terms and conditions that stop you from using these technologies in whatever manner is required,” Taneja told Al Jazeera.

items.text:
Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
- Published
Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.
Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.
In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu.
The family did not disclose the cause of his death, although local media reported that the Nollywood star had been in poor health in recent months.
Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.
His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.
He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.
Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.
"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.
Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.
He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

items.text:
The Gambia election: Can the next president deliver on a decade of promise
Gambians head to the polls amid economic hardship and unfulfilled promises of reform and justice.
Banjul, The Gambia – As Gambians prepare to vote on December 5, unemployment, rising living costs, unreliable public services and delayed justice are testing the country’s democratic transition. Nearly a decade after Yahya Jammeh’s departure, voters are asking whether the next president can deliver the change they were promised.
For Sosseh Jagne, the election is about more than who occupies the State House. It is about whether the next government can create conditions in which Gambians can earn a living.
Jagne established Ya Anna’s Catering in 2020 and expanded it into a restaurant in early 2025. But frequent electricity outages have disrupted her business, affecting food preparation, refrigeration and customer service. Between August and October, she said, power cuts sometimes lasted 19 hours or longer.
She estimates that spoiled food cost her more than 40,000 Gambian dalasis ($532). She has also stopped selling homemade iced juices because she cannot guarantee they will remain properly chilled.
“Electricity is not a luxury; it is a necessity for people’s everyday lives and, especially, for businesses that depend on it to operate,” she told Al Jazeera.
Her experience reflects the pressures facing households and businesses as President Adama Barrow seeks a third term. He is one of eight candidates in the December 5 election, according to the Independent Electoral Commission. Barrow came to power in 2017 after defeating Jammeh, who ruled the country for 22 years.
The cost of survival
For many young Gambians, the central question is where they can find work.
The 2025 Gambia Labour Force Survey puts overall unemployment at 8.3 percent, up from 7.6 percent in 2022–23. Among people aged 15 to 35, unemployment stands at 11.5 percent. The survey also found that 41.3 percent of young people in that age group were neither employed nor in education or training.
For 26-year-old Maram Mendy, a graduate of the University of The Gambia, finding a job has become increasingly discouraging. Her parents sacrificed to finance her education, making her inability to find work particularly difficult.
“I’m now fed up with looking for a job,” she told Al Jazeera.
She said employers frequently demand previous experience, leaving graduates caught in a cycle: They cannot get a job without experience, but cannot gain experience without employment.
For 28-year-old Buba Sanneh, unemployed since graduating in 2023, the frustration has prompted thoughts of travelling to Europe through irregular migration, commonly known as the backway.
For Hakeem Touray, the search for opportunities abroad has already cost his family dearly. His elder brother, Bob, was 27 when he attempted the journey to Europe in 2021. He died trying to cross the Mediterranean Sea.
Hakeem said the loss highlighted the consequences of unemployment, poverty and limited opportunities at home.
The risks are reflected in figures cited by UN Special Rapporteur Morris Tidball-Binz, following his visit to The Gambia in October 2026. In his end-of-mission statement, he said independent sources had reported that 1,603 Gambians died attempting irregular migration in 2024 and 893 in 2025, most of them at sea. Separately, the International Organization for Migration had recorded at least 408 Gambians missing along migration routes since 2014.
For families, these are not simply statistics but lives lost and loved ones whose fate remains uncertain.
Living costs and basic services
Economic hardship extends beyond unemployment. According to figures published by the Gambia Bureau of Statistics, 53.4 percent of the population – about 1.1 million people – lived below the national poverty line in 2020. The rate was particularly high in rural areas, at about 76 percent, compared with 34 percent in urban areas.
At Bakoteh Market, 38-year-old vegetable seller Fatoumatta Jawara said rising prices have made supporting her family increasingly difficult. She also wants affordable healthcare to become a priority.
“Survival is becoming harder with each passing day. We need a president who will improve our lives for the better,” she told Al Jazeera.
Nearby, 22-year-old Isatou Ceesay, a mother of two, said she had grown tired of politicians’ promises.
“All they do is promise, and after the election you don’t hear from them again. We are tired of their endless promises,” she said.
Security is another concern, particularly in communities near Senegal’s Casamance region. Instability in the neighbouring region has raised concerns about the safety of border communities and the livelihoods that depend on cross-border movement.
The unfinished promise of justice
For families affected by abuses under Jammeh, the 2017 change of government brought hopes of accountability. Nearly a decade later, many are still waiting.
Sainabou Camara Lowe was 17 when security forces violently suppressed student demonstrations in April 2000, leaving more than a dozen students dead. She survived, but sustained a spinal injury that required two operations.
Now 43 and widowed, she raises five children while struggling with limited mobility. Although she received about 900,000 dalasis ($11,970) through the reparations process, she said the payment had done little to ease her family’s hardship.
“We are forgotten as victims and continue to wallow in pain and poverty,” she told Al Jazeera.
Kebba Jome, national coordinator of the Gambia Centre for Victims of Human Rights Violations, said fewer than 25 percent of the 263 recommendations made by the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission had been fully implemented.
A special tribunal to prosecute alleged crimes committed under Jammeh is expected to begin hearings early next year, Jome said. He argued that the next president would have a responsibility to ensure the accountability process mov
