items.text:
Kilmar Ábrego García leaving US for Spain, ending Trump deportation battle
- Published
Kilmar Ábrego García, whose deportation last year to El Salvador sparked a bitter deportation battle, is leaving the US for Spain.
He is set to take a commercial flight to the country on Tuesday, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
After the government admitted it had wrongfully sent Ábrego García to his home country, he was returned to the US to face human trafficking charges, which were later dropped. The administration then continued its attempts to send him to other countries, including Uganda and Ghana.
His deportation and return became a flashpoint in the debate over President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
Ábrego García, who is married to a US citizen and lived in Maryland, came to the US illegally from El Salvador as a teenager.
Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, visited Ábrego García while he was in the notorious Cecot prison in El Salvador in 2025 and advocated for his release.
"A year and a half ago, the Trump Administration wanted to leave Kilmar Ábrego García to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Van Hollen said in a statement on Tuesday. "Today, Kilmar is travelling to a country of his choice, a free man - unharmed and with dignity."
In a statement, Ábrego García's lawyer said his departure was "temporary" as he had "many options to return to the United States".
"We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," the statement said.
"Where he goes from here, where he chooses to settle for the next two years while he waits out the end of this administration, will be his choice, not the administration's choice."
The BBC has contacted the US Department of Homeland Security for comment.
Ábrego García was arrested in 2019 alongside three other men and detained by federal immigration authorities. A judge granted him protection from deportation to El Salvador at the time, citing the risk of persecution by a gang there.
In March 2025, the Trump administration deported him to El Salvador, where he was held in Cecot, a prison known for its harsh conditions. The US Supreme Court then ordered the government to facilitate his return.
The administration admitted that he was deported in error and brought him back to the US where he was set to face human trafficking charges. A federal judge dismissed the case, saying Ábrego García had been charged for political reasons.
For months, he was locked in a battle over deportation with the government.
Ábrego García had repeatedly said he would be willing to be deported to Costa Rica, and the Costa Rican government had agreed to accept him as a refugee and provide him with legal status.
After reports emerged that the administration was considering sending him to Uganda, a judge barred the government from deporting Ábrego García to a third country.
At one point the Trump administration requested that the judge lift the order so that Ábrego García could be deported to Liberia, CBS reported.

UK warns companies of potential Russian sabotage threat

Britain’s Defence Ministry and the country’s security service, known as MI5, are warning companies that support Ukraine’s milita
items.text:
UK warns companies of potential Russian sabotage threat
Britain’s Defence Ministry and the country’s security service warn of the threat in an unusual public announcement.
Britain’s Defence Ministry and the country’s security service, known as MI5, are warning companies that support Ukraine’s military that they may face attempted sabotage from Russia.
“If your organisation supports military procurement or supplies equipment to Ukraine’s armed forces, it could be a target,” the Ministry of Defence and the National Protective Security Authority said in an unusual public announcement on Tuesday.
“This activity is typically characterised by the use of proxy actors employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson,” the warning said, urging companies to take action against security threats posed by what they described as operatives acting for Russia.
‘No plans to attack the UK’
Russia’s embassy in London denied such claims in a statement and said: “Russia has no plans, reasons or intentions to attack the UK.”
It also accused Ukraine of carrying out sabotage to “put the blame on Russia and extort more money from western governments”, something Kyiv has repeatedly denied.
Since the Ukraine war started and Britain became one of Kyiv’s key supporters, London has accused Russia of being behind a number of spying and sabotage plots.
Last year, three British men were convicted for an arson attack on a warehouse storing Starlink satellite equipment bound for Ukraine, which prosecutors said was carried out by Russian military intelligence agents.
In September, a man was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service after alleged contact with Russian military spies.
On Sunday, Estonia said it would close all its border crossing points with Russia following a suspected sabotage attack on an Estonian defence company, while last week the Norwegian security service said it expected Russian intelligence to carry out sabotage attacks in Norway in the coming year.
UK closed-door security briefings
Britain’s Ministry of Defence said it was holding closed-door security briefings with leaders from the critical national infrastructure and defence sectors over the next two days to advise on security.
“Recent sabotage attempts right across Europe demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face,” Security Minister Dan Jarvis said.
“It’s truly shameful that actors are seeking to disrupt our way of life and that of our allies, especially targeting organisations doing vital work in support of Ukraine.”

items.text:
India news: Trump administration set to unveil new tariffs after probe
Published November 25, 2026last updated November 25, 2026
What you need to know
- USTR set to unveil results of a probe on excess industrial capacity in India and 15 other economies
- Probe could lead to fresh tariffs on India and others
- Woman allegedly gangraped in Delhi by her colleagues
Here are the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, November 25:
Woman gang raped by colleagues in east Delhi, three held
Three people have been arrested after a 22-year-old woman alleged she was gang-raped by two men, with assistance from others, at a cafe in east Delhi, local media said citing police sources.
Police were currently making efforts to trace three others who were absconding.
News agency Press Trust of India reported that the incident took place when the victim gathered at the cafe with six colleagues on Monday night for a party. The cafe had shut for the day before midnight on Monday but the group entered after hours as they had the keys to the establishment. News channel NDTV reported that the victim and her colleagues worked at the very cafe.
Delhi Police has launched a formal investigation against four men and two women under India's criminal law. Three suspects, including at least one woman, have been arrested so far.
This comes just less than two months after a woman was gang-raped in a public park in Delhi, triggering public anger and protests. Women's safety remains a contentious issue in India with frequent headlines of violence against women in the news.
US set to unveil new tariffs after probe on excess factory capacity
India could be one of the 16 countries facing fresh and imminent US tariffs with the Trump administration set to release the findings of a probe aimed at countering alleged excess industrial capacities, Reuters reported citing three people with knowledge of the matter.
The results of the investigation are likely to be released over the course of the day, followed by new import duties on a wide range of goods if the probe find India guilty of excess capacity.
It remains unclear what tariff rates would be proposed but one of the sources told the news agency that they would be specifically tailored to each country.
That said, the US is likely to honor capped tariff rates agreed on in finalized US trade deals with partner countries.
A report by the Wall Street Journal said that India could face higher US tariffs than economies like Japan or the European Union.
Where are US tariffs on India?
The US introduced 25% reciprocal tariffs in 2025 on India, under US President Donald Trump's second term. The rate was later lowered to 18% with Washington and New Delhi agreeing to an interim trade framework while a more comprehensive trade agreement would be worked on. Leaders from both nations have since said the first tranche of a trade agreement was "close," but a deal remains elusive.
Meanwhile in July 2026, the United States Trade Representative (USTR), which carries out trade-related investigations, imposed an additional 10% tariffs on India and other countries after a probe on traded goods made using forced labor.
Welcome to our coverage
Good morning! and welcome to DW's India blog.
This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from Studio Delhi and I will be your guide through India's news cycle.
The national capital once again woke up to the news of an alleged gang-rape in east Delhi where a woman was assaulted by her colleagues on Monday night. Local media reports say at least one of the three held is a woman, while three others remain absconding.
In other news, India is among a bunch of countries that might face fresh US tariffs under a trade investigation. US President Donald Trump's administration has been using trade probes as a proxy to reciprocal tariffs. The results of the latest probe are expected soon.
Stay tuned for this and more.

items.text:
Libya: 2 dead after Ukrainian attack on Russian warship in Benghazi
November 25, 2026
Two Libyan soldiers have died from their injuries sustained during a Ukrainian attack on a Russian warship in docked in the port of Benghazi.
Libya is currently divided between a UN-recognized government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east of the country that controls Benghazi.
The head of the eastern administration, Oussama Hamad, said the two men had died "as a result of their injuries during the treacherous Ukrainian aggression against the port of Benghazi."
The Libyan National Army General Command said a response would come "at the appropriate time and place."
Earlier, on Monday, Libya's Foreign ministry denounced the attacks and said it didn't authorize "any foreign military operations within [Libya's] territory or territorial waters.
Ukraine denies dragging Libya into war
The naval drone attack that occurred on Sunday was claimed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday. On Tuesday, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha defended the attack.
"Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Sybiha said on Telegram.
"Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended ‌to harm Libya or its people."
He said Russia was the one endangering third countries by using their civilian infrastrure for military purposes.
According to the Institute for the Study of War, the Russian corvette warship had stopped for several days in Benghazi's port to refuel and resupply.
Another Ukrainian naval drone attack on Sunday sank a Russian-owned container ship that was allegedly transporting military equipment.
Ukraine has in recent months sought to attack Russian targets further and further away, including a series of strikes in Siberia.

items.title: Amnesty calls for ICC genocide probe over Israel's impact on births in Gaza
items.summary:
Amnesty calls for ICC genocide probe over Israel's impact on births in Gaza
Amnesty International is urging the International Criminal Court to investigate whether Israeli officials committed genocide in Gaza, citing measures it says have prevented births and severely harmed women's reproductive hea
items.text:
Amnesty calls for ICC genocide probe over Israel's impact on births in Gaza
Amnesty International is urging the International Criminal Court to investigate whether Israeli officials committed genocide in Gaza, citing measures it says have prevented births and severely harmed women's reproductive health. The rights group said it had serious concerns that these effects were intentional, while acknowledging it could not reach a definitive conclusion.
Amnesty International accused Israel on Wednesday of imposing measures that prevented births in Gaza, while its chief called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to investigate the possible "commission of genocide".
In a report published Wednesday on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, Amnesty paints a bleak picture of the consequences of the war that began in October 2023 for the physical, mental and reproductive health of women in Gaza.
From then until October 2026, "Israel's actions have prevented access to fertility treatment and contributed to pregnancy complications, including miscarriage and stillbirth," Amnesty International Secretary General Agnès Callamard said at a press conference.
The report expresses "serious concerns that this outcome was intentional", but acknowledges that it is "not in a position to conclude this categorically".
Contacted by AFP, COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry body in charge of civilian matters in the Palestinian territories, accused Amnesty of "echoing Hamas's false narratives".
It said more than 27,000 tonnes of medical equipment and medicine have entered Gaza since a US-brokered ceasefire began in October 2025 and that 35 hospitals were operational, including "women's health and fertility facilities".
The report details cases of women and girls killed or injured in Israeli attacks while seeking medical care or while in maternity wards in Gaza.
Many women went through pregnancy or tended to their newborns despite their injuries under relentless bombardment, the report says.
Shortages of medical equipment have also compromised pregnancy monitoring, obstetric and postnatal care, as well as the diagnosis of complications, according to Amnesty.
It added that shortages of anaesthetics and medicines needed to treat haemorrhaging during childbirth have sometimes had fatal consequences.
Amnesty attributed the shortages to Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, which "contribute to rising maternal and neonatal mortality".
In light of these conclusions, Callamard called on the ICC to "consider the commission of genocide by Israeli officials since October 2023" and to include in its investigation "gender-based crimes and reproductive harms".
"Measures intended to prevent births" within a group constitute an act of genocide when undertaken with the "intent to destroy, in whole or in part, that group", according to Article II of the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
No treatment available
Among the 228 interviews conducted for the report, two paramedics told Amnesty of two incidents that occurred in early 2026, a few hundred metres from the so-called Yellow Line demarcating the area under Israeli control in the Gaza Strip.
In both cases, a woman about to give birth and the ambulance dispatched to collect her came under fire, according to their testimony.
The report also cites the case of a 20-day-old infant who died in 2025 from an infection contracted after sharing an incubator with another sick baby.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war sparked by Hamas's unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack, according to Gaza's health ministry, which operates under Hamas but whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The ministry also reported a roughly 41 percent drop in the number of live births in the first half of 2025 compared with 2022. The UN also recorded a decline in the number of deliveries in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period the previous year.
The NGO also said it has "found evidence" of the use of hospitals "by Palestinian armed groups", notably to hold hostages or for the "torture of Palestinians", but has found no evidence supporting Israeli accusations of their use as Hamas command centres.
Amnesty also said that before the war, Gaza had at least nine clinics offering in vitro fertilisation (IVF) but none now provide these treatments.
"Thousands of stored embryos, sperm and eggs were destroyed," it said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
Keywords for this article

items.title: Colombia’s president arrives at scene of supermarket hostage siege in tourist city
items.summary:
Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city.
Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse
items.text:
Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city.
Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported, where he will ostensibly take control of a operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.
About 30 people were initially seized by the armed men early on Tuesday morning, but by nightfall, 10 hostages – five of them elderly women – had been released, police said.
There have been no reports of injuries so far.
Before arriving in Cartagena, the right-wing president said that, despite the context of growing violence perpetrated by criminal groups involved in the country’s decades-long armed conflict, the hostage-taking appeared to have stemmed from a botched robbery carried out by “common criminals”.
The past few days have been particularly challenging in the South American country, with a car bomb and a drone attack killing one person and leaving nearly 30 injured.
The supermarket where the hostages are being held is just six miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls overlooking the Caribbean. Hundreds of thousands of visitors are drawn to Cartagena every year.
The gunmen reportedly arrived at about 8.30am local time at an Éxito supermarket in La Castellana neighbourhood and, according to Colombia’s president, the group planned to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle that was due to collect the previous day’s takings from the store.
After spotting the movement on security cameras, employees reportedly alerted the national police, who surrounded the supermarket.
“My son is there,” Jacob Perez, the father of one of the workers reportedly held hostage, told Agence France-Presse. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him,” he said.
Customers were also believed to be among the hostages. The five people initially released were “older women”, according to De la Espriella.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the supermarket, while local media outlets showed snipers positioned on nearby buildings in what appeared to be a standoff between the armed men and police.
De la Espriella, known for his populist rhetoric and an “iron fist” approach to crime – he sometimes wears a gun on his waist and has posed beside the bodies of people killed by police – has been in office for just over three months, and said the hours-long standoff at the supermarket “will turn out well for the hostages, but I’m not so sure it will turn out quite so well for the hostage-takers”.
He addressed the case at a press conference in Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he was dealing with the aftermath of an attack on Monday night in which a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).
“Narco-terrorism is desperate because we are confronting it decisively. It intends to intimidate us and force us to retreat in search of another false peace process,” the president said, referring to the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc – whose signing marked its 10th anniversary on Tuesday.
Internationally recognised for substantially reducing violence, the deal alone could not bring the decades-long armed conflict to a definitive end. Subsequent administrations were slow to implement the agreement, which was rejected by Farc dissidents and other rebel factions.
In the early hours of Monday, in another part of the country, gunmen believed to belong to the ELN, an armed group that never signed a peace deal, used drones to drop bombs on the local police command in the city of Cúcuta. Instead they hit homes and injured three civilians, including an 18-month-old baby.
Although drone attacks by criminal groups have become increasingly common, it was the first time they had targeted a departmental capital.

items.title: IEBC Enlists Digital Creators in Voter Education Campaign
items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission is seeking to leverage the growing influence of social media to expand voter education and reach young Kenyans ahead of the 2027 General Election.
IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon said digital platforms had become influentia
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission is seeking to leverage the growing influence of social media to expand voter education and reach young Kenyans ahead of the 2027 General Election.
IEBC Chairperson Erastus Ethekon said digital platforms had become influential in shaping public opinion, making content creators important partners in communicating electoral information.
“The engagement recognised the growing influence of digital platforms in shaping public opinion, particularly among young people, and the important role content creators can play in sharing electoral information, addressing misconceptions and encouraging informed participation in the democratic process,” Ethekon said.
He reaffirmed the commission’s readiness to provide influencers with accurate and timely information to enable them to develop credible and engaging content on electoral processes.
Ethekon said sustained collaboration would help ensure Kenyans receive reliable information as the country approaches the next General Election.
He urged them to reject tribalism, hate speech, incitement and divisive narratives, and instead use their influence to build bridges, foster understanding and bring Kenyans together despite their political, ethnic and social differences.
The meeting focused on opportunities for cooperation in voter education, public awareness and the promotion of national cohesion.

                                Two Libyan soldiers have died from injuries sustained in an attack, claimed by Ukraine, on Russian ships near Benghazi, a senior figure in the administration in eastern Libya said late on Tuesday. Members of the European Parliament will convene in Strasbourg on Wednesday to discuss 'Europe’s role and capacity to protect the international order and secure a just and lasting peace for Ukraine.' Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.            
                                                    
        
                    
                                    
                        North Korea expels Swiss diplomat over sanctions on camp accused of indoctrinating Ukrainian children
North Korea's foreign ministry ordered the head of Switzerland's diplomatic office to leave the country within 48 hours, state media said Wednesday, a day after Pyongyang threatened to shut the newly opened office in retaliation for Swiss sanctions.
"The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours," Pyongyang's official Korean Central News Agency said.
On Tuesday, the powerful sister of North Korea's leader threatened to close Switzerland's diplomatic office, denouncing new Swiss sanctions on a camp in the North Korean city of Wonsan attended by Chinese and Russian children.
The Songdowon International Children's Camp has been accused of helping to indoctrinate Ukrainian children brought from Russian-occupied territories.
Switzerland – where both Kim Jong Un and Kim Yo Jong studied – sanctioned the camp on 4 November, accusing it of participating in the "transfer of Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine" to North Korea and contributing to "efforts aimed at the ideological conditioning and russification of Ukrainian children".
                                    
                                                
                    
                        Two Libyan soldiers die from injuries sustained in attack on Russian vessels
Two Libyan soldiers have died from injuries sustained in an attack, claimed by Ukraine, on Russian ships near Benghazi, a senior figure in the administration in eastern Libya said late on Tuesday.
Libya is divided between a UN-recognized government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east of the country, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.
Haftar's camp has maintained close military and strategic ties with Russia for several years.
His son Saddam Haftar, who is widely seen as heir apparent, said "it is with deep sadness and great pride that I pay tribute today to two heroes of our naval forces," following the attack.
They "were martyred as a result of their injuries sustained during the performance of their national duty following the criminal attack on the Benghazi Naval Base", he added on Facebook.
                            
            
   - A Russian attack killed two people and wounded 22 more, including two children, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia overnight, Ivan ‌Fedorov, co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Defense Council, said on Telegram.
- Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on its drone attacks against a Russian military vessel and cargo ship in Libyan waters at the weekend was a legitimate act of self-defence, following criticism from the government in Tripoli.
- More than 500,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war with Ukraine, according to an estimate by a number of media organisations. The figures are based on a huge dataset that was hacked from Russia’s state statistics agency Rosstat by Belarusian activist group Cyber Partisans and Ukrainian hacker group Silent Crow.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

items.text:
Asia’s stock markets dive as doubts swirl over AI boom
Markets fall sharply in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan in latest tech-led sell-off.
Asian stock markets have fallen sharply as doubts continue to swirl over the AI boom, reversing a rally sparked by Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia.
Taiwan’s stock market led the sell-off, with the benchmark Taiex plunging as much as 7.9 percent in morning trading.
South Korea’s Kospi fell more than 6 percent, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 3.6 percent.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index bucked the trend, rising by as much as 1.3 percent.
Tech stocks linked to AI trade suffered some of the steepest losses.
In Japan, Tokyo Electron, a leading manufacturer of semiconductor fabrication equipment, dived 13.5 percent, while Advantest, a producer of chip testing equipment, plunged 14.5 percent.
South Korea’s Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the top two global memory chip makers, sank 9.1 percent and 9.9 percent, respectively.
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s biggest contract chip maker, and Taiwanese Apple supplier Foxconn both dropped more than 9 percent.
AI headwinds
The retreat comes after Asian markets surged on Tuesday following Huang’s surprise reinstatement at the helm of chip giant Nvidia after an intervention by US President Donald Trump.
Nvidia’s reappointment of Huang, who resigned amid claims he was romantically involved with a woman suspected of working with Chinese intelligence, sent the chip giant’s New York-listed shares 31.5 percent higher, the largest single-day gain in US stock market history.
Wall Street saw modest losses on Tuesday after the previous session’s buying spree, with the S&P 500 falling 0.5 percent and the Nasdaq composite down 1.5 percent.
Markets have seen wild swings over the past month amid the Nvidia scandal and expectations that Democrats in Washington, DC, will push for greater regulation of AI following their sweeping victories in the US midterm elections.
Those headwinds have added to existing concerns that tech firms may not be able to sustain their multi-trillion-dollar investments underpinning the AI boom.
Big Tech’s debt-fuelled splurge has stirred intense debate about whether it is investing in a future gold mine or a massive stock market bubble.
Global AI-related investment is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $3.6 trillion in 2027, according to technology insights company Gartner.

items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 11 – German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has arrived in Kenya for an official visit expected to strengthen bilateral relations between Nairobi and Berlin.
Steinmeier was received at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport by Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign Affairs Cabinet Sec
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 11 – German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has arrived in Kenya for an official visit expected to strengthen bilateral relations between Nairobi and Berlin.
Steinmeier was received at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport by Prime Cabinet Secretary and Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi.
“I look forward to the high-level bilateral discussions with President William Ruto, aimed at advancing our shared priorities and opening new avenues for mutually beneficial cooperation,” Mudavadi stated.
Mudavadi said the visit presented an opportunity for the two countries to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, clean energy, climate action, education, technology and skills development.
In a statement following the president’s arrival, Mudavadi described Kenya and Germany as longstanding partners whose relations are anchored on mutual trust, economic cooperation and a shared commitment to sustainable development.
He said strengthening bilateral ties could unlock additional investment, create employment and training opportunities for young Kenyans and facilitate the exchange of knowledge and technology.
Mudavadi also expressed anticipation for high-level bilateral discussions between Steinmeier and President William Ruto, saying the engagements would focus on advancing shared priorities and identifying new areas of cooperation.
“Kenya and Germany share a longstanding partnership built on mutual trust, economic cooperation and a common vision for sustainable development,” Mudavadi said.

items.text:
China launches Shenzhou-24 to Tiangong station
November 25, 2026
The Shenzhou-24 spacecraft lifted off on a Long March-2F rocket at 8:18 am local time (0018 GMT) from the Jiuquan launch center in the Gobi Desert.
The China Manned Space Agency reported that the capsule separated from the rocket about 10 minutes later and entered orbit, and called the launch a "complete success".
State broadcaster CCTV showed the three crew members leafing through a manual minutes after liftoff and reported that they were in good condition.
What do we know about the crew?
Tang Hongbo is making his third trip to space. CCTV said he will become the first astronaut to board Tiangong three times. Wu Yi is on his first flight, as is Pakistani pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to fly on a Chinese crewed mission.
"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.
The handover on the station will be unusual. Shenzhou-23 commander Zhu Yangzhu will remain on board for a year, while the rest of his crew — Lai Ka-ying, Hong Kong's first astronaut, and Zhang Zhiyuan — return to Earth with Ali.
Zhu's stay is reportedly China's first full-year spell in space. Reuters said it will be the longest single stay by a Chinese astronaut. It has been described as a test of how the human body copes, ahead of planned Moon missions and possibly a journey to Mars.
What is on the agenda?
The crew will carry out more than 90 experiments and technology tests, Xinhua reported. At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology had made teamwork harder, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
Ali, speaking in Mandarin, told reporters: "It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights."
China's 2030 target for a crewed Moon landing is unchanged despite the delay to its Chang'e-7 lunar mission. The United States is aiming for 2028.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was wrongfully deported to El Salvador last year as part of United States President Donald Trump’s immi
items.text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia self-deports to Spain after lengthy US legal battle
US Senator Chris Van Hollen hails Kilmar Abrego Garcia’s safe departure to Spain as a ‘free man’.
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was wrongfully deported to El Salvador last year as part of United States President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has self-deported to Spain.
Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national, voluntarily departed on Tuesday after months of legal opposition to a second deportation, this time to one of various African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.
A judge told Abrego Garcia to self-deport on Tuesday, The Associated Press reported, citing a source familiar with the matter.
US Senator Chris Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia while pressing for his release from Salvadoran mega-prison CECOT, said Abrego Garcia is “traveling to a country of his choice, a free man”.
“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free – including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” Van Hollen, who is vying for Senate majority leader, said in a statement posted on X.
Salvadoran prison
Abrego Garcia, 31, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a Salvadoran prison notorious for abusive conditions and alleged use of torture.
The Trump administration, at the time, described Abrego Garcia’s deportation as an “administrative error”. However, the administration initially refused to seek his return, arguing that Abrego Garcia was a member of the MS-13 gang despite having no criminal record at the time of his removal.
In June 2025, the Trump administration brought him back after facing public pressure and a court order, but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee.
The Tennessee case was dismissed by a federal judge in May, though the government appealed it in August.
Abrego Garcia had said that if he must be deported, he would prefer to be sent to Costa Rica, but Todd Lyons, the former acting director of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said that deporting him to Costa Rica would be “prejudicial to the United States” in a March 2026 memo.
Lyons wrote that Abrego Garcia should be sent to Liberia because the US has spent government resources and political capital negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals.
The memo came despite a US agreement with Costa Rica to accept deportees who cannot legally be returned to their home countries.
Abrego Garcia has lived in Maryland for years, but he immigrated to the US illegally as a teenager.
In 2019, an immigration judge issued an order saying that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced danger there from a gang that had threatened his family.
The judge allowed him to live and work in the US under ICE supervision, but he was not given residency status.

World Health ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has called for the lifting of a US fuel blockade on Cuba, as shortages dent t
items.text:
WHO chief urges end to US fuel blockade on Cuba
UN allocates $2m for immunisation, medical equipment as Cuban healthcare struggles with critical shortages.
World Health ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has called for the lifting of a US fuel blockade on Cuba, as shortages dent the island’s once vaunted healthcare system.
Tedros warned that the sanctions were endangering the lives of children on Tuesday, during a visit to Cuba that included tours of several healthcare facilities in Havana.
“The intensification of fuel restrictions and sanctions is causing direct harm to the Cuban people, especially the most vulnerable,” Tedros said.
During his three-day visit, the United Nations health agency’s top official said his organisation would contribute $2m to help strengthen Cuba’s ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌national immunisation programme and provide essential medical equipment to healthcare facilities.
The UN has repeatedly warned of a growing humanitarian crisis on the island, calling the US blockade a violation of international law and the human rights of all Cubans.
Cuba’s government says the measures led to daily power outages lasting 20 hours or more, critical shortages of medicines and surgical supplies, and a decline in health indicators, such as infant mortality rates.
Tedros met with Cuba’s President Miguel Diaz-Canel on Tuesday to discuss the country’s health needs.
“We agreed on the need to prioritise essential health services and time-sensitive interventions, particularly for children,” Tedros wrote in a post on X.
“Fuel restrictions and sanctions affecting the purchase of medical products are severely impacting the health system that Cuban doctors have built over decades.”
Falling life expectancy
Tedros said during a news conference that Cuba’s life expectancy had fallen from 78.8 years in 2020 to 74.4 years in 2025, the first decline since records began in 1950.
The 2025 figures predate the imposition by the administration of US President Donald Trump of a fuel blockade and stiff sanctions against a ‌number of Cuban officials and entities in January.
Washington argues the energy blockade is intended to push for political change on the island and says that exports of food and medicine are subject to legal exemptions.
An annual non-binding resolution calling for an end to a US embargo on the island has ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌passed ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌in favour of Cuba in the UN General Assembly by wide margins every year since 1992.

A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei on a slew of charges on Tuesday including stealing trade secrets and violating sanctions.
The jury in the Brooklyn federal court found the company guilty on 10 of th
items.text:
US jury convicts Huawei of violating sanctions, stealing trade secrets
November 25, 2026
A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei on a slew of charges on Tuesday including stealing trade secrets and violating sanctions.
The jury in the Brooklyn federal court found the company guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts that it faced, which also included bank fraud and wire fraud.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said after the verdict.
However, the jury acquitted Huawei on two charges of racketeering and conspiring to obstruct justice.
The verdict is the latest blow to the Chinese tech giant which has for years been banned from selling networking devices to telecom carries in the US and other Western countries. However, its consumer electronics business has continued to grow as its networking business in other countries.
Stolen source code, antenna technology and robot tech
Prosecutors detailed a number of ways Huawei stole trade secrets from competitors in order to undercut them in the market.
In once instance, a Huawei employee slipped into a competitor's booth at a Chicago trade fair in order to photograph circuitboards inside another company's networking divice.
Huawei was also found to have once sold routers containing source code from a rival company.
Prosecutors also said a Huawei employee once removed a robotic arm from a competitor's lab so it could be photographed and measured.
According to court records, the victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu.
"The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology," the Department of Justice said.
False statenments about Iran operations
Prosecutors also alleged that Huawei did business in countries subject to US sanctions including Iran and North Korea.
Huawei then made false statements to both US government officials and banks in order to hide this activity, prosecutors said.
"Few crimes are as serious as Huawei's decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the ‌enforcement of US laws," US Attorney Joseph Nocella said.
Huawei to appeal verdict
Huawei continued to deny the allegations even after the verdict on Tuesday.
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," the company said in a statement.
"The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades. No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation."
The company's lawyer, Brian Heberlig, said: "We fully expect to appeal."
Huawei is set to be sentenced next September and could face billions of dollars in penalties.

Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materia
items.text:
Thomas Markle indicted in US for possessing child sex abuse images
- Published
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex has been indicted by a federal grand jury in Los Angeles for possessing child sex abuse images.
Markle, who remains in custody in Florida, allegedly possessed materials that include at least one image involving a prepubescent minor and a minor under 12 years old, court documents filed in California show.
The 82-year-old has denied possessing images of child sex abuse. He is expected to be arraigned in Los Angeles in the coming weeks.
Last week, a judge in Florida declared Prince Harry's father-in-law mentally competent to stand trial.
The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home in Florida on a single federal charge of possessing child sexual abuse material. He now faces two counts.
US attorney Bill Essayli said Markle faces a maximum of 20 years in prison on each count if convicted.
His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles for almost two decades uncovered the abuse material.
Markle was initially released on conditional bail but was then ordered to stay in jail pending trial after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.
In the indictment, filed by the US Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, Markle is accused of knowingly possessing 35mm film negatives on 30 October and 4 November that contained child sexual abuse materials.
The US Attorney's Office said that during both instances Markle allegedly knew the images contained such materials.
Inside the storage units, federal agents found two images that depict an adult man - whom a witness identified as Markle - with an underage child, the US attorney's office said.
They also alleged that a third image appears to depict a child in a room believed to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Markle moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and he lived in Cebu until May.
"The affidavit also describes additional photographs that appear to show Markle with children in various stages of undress," prosecutors said.

Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has announced an agreement to unite with a right-wing opposition party in a bid to
items.text:
Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
The Yashar party says it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party, led by Avigdor Lieberman.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has announced an agreement to unite with a right-wing opposition party in a bid to form the next Israeli government following October’s elections.
The Yashar party said on Tuesday that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel’s Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
After no party managed to secure a 61-seat majority, Israel’s parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, while Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister despite the October 27 election stripping Netanyahu of his majority.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
Arab parties
The agreement between Eisenkot, whose party won 21 parliament seats, and Lieberman, whose party won seven, was unforeseen since Lieberman has been vocal about his opposition to forming a government with support from Arab parties as well as to a unity government with Netanyahu.
Lieberman had once served as foreign minister under a previous Netanyahu government but has since become a strong critic.
Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud’s alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties outperformed election expectations but still lost its majority. It now holds 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners, including Lieberman, hold just 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel’s Arab minority, which hold 19 seats and are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
The path forward
Talks are also ongoing between Eisenkot, some of his “change bloc” partners and Likud on forming a unity government.
The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot after the Yashar party leader’s talks with Netanyahu’s Likud on a possible unity government.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with Arab parties.

items.title: Pep 'embarrassed' to turn down Italy job, says national team 'next step'
items.summary:
Pep Guardiola said he felt "embarrassed" to turn down the head coaching position with Italy, but added he could return to coaching in the future and, if he did, would like to do it with a national team.
In the end, Guardiola said in an interview on Romario TV on Tuesday that he passed on the Italy j
items.text:
Pep Guardiola said he felt "embarrassed" to turn down the head coaching position with Italy, but added he could return to coaching in the future and, if he did, would like to do it with a national team.
In the end, Guardiola said in an interview on Romario TV on Tuesday that he passed on the Italy job because he needed to take a break following his departure from Manchester City after 10 years.
A trophy-laden decade in the dugout from 2016 to 2026 at City that included six Premier League titles, three FA Cups and a Champions League crown, left Guardiola exhausted and forced him to take a self-imposed sabbatical of at least one year.
Soon after, though, Guardiola was approached by Paolo Maldini and Leonardo, who were working on behalf of the Italian federation in its search for a new coach, to gauge his interest in taking over the top spot for the Azzurri after they had missed out on the World Cup for a third consecutive time.
"This is the first time I speak about this, but yes, I did talk to them," Guardiola told Brazil legend and former Barcelona teammate Romario on his show. "I felt embarrassed to say 'no' to Italy, a country like Italy, it would have been one of the greatest honors of my career to coach the Italian national team. But I realized I needed to stop. If they had called two years earlier, I probably would have accepted. But when Paolo Maldini and Leonardo, whom I love dearly, reached out, it was at a point where I simply had to stop.
"I needed some time for myself. After 18 years as a coach, with matches every three days, week in and week out, there comes a moment when you just have to say 'phew.'"
Italy ultimately hired Roberto Mancini, who had already managed the team from 2018 to 2023 and led it to the 2020 European Championship.
The former Barcelona and Bayern Munich manager did not rule out a return to coaching, saying that when he does it will be because "someone wants me."
As to where that might be, Guardiola said he didn't know, but that if there was one team he never coached but would have liked to it was "a national team," adding "and that is the next step."
Guardiola was rumored to be a target for U.S. Soccer as it looked for a new manager to replace Mauricio Pochettino after the Argentine left the United States for Manchester United.
Around the time of Pochettino's departure, ESPN sources said U.S. Soccer's search was "expected to include former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola," though a federation source cautioned that it was premature to call Guardiola the top target.
On his way out, Pochettino was asked about a possible succession plan centered on Guardiola and he said it was "the perfect moment to arrive" at the USMNT.
"Everything is in the right direction. I think, of course, take [it]," Pochettino said in his last news conference as U.S. coach. "Take it because [Guardiola is] going to find really good people, good players. The player can fit for his style; the National Training Center that wasn't [there] before."
During Italy's pursuit of Guardiola in July, an ESPN source also confirmed Guardiola's interest in coaching a national team but could not confirm the countries. The source added that the Netherlands, who recently hired Xavi, and England, managed by Thomas Tuchel, have both been credited with an interest in the Catalan coach.
For now, Guardiola says he is content on the sidelines.
"The truth is, I don't know, I really don't know. But for now, I'm doing fine," Guardiola said Tuesday. "If I ever return, it will be because my gut tells me to, and because someone wants me, then I we'll go back. But it's been many years, so many matches."
ESPN Brazil contributed to this report.

items.title: Bellingham credits Mourinho 'full stop' for stellar form after Madrid stunner
items.summary:
Jude Bellingham praised José Mourinho for helping him reach career-best form after the midfielder scored a stunning goal in Real Madrid's 5-1 comeback win over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.
Madrid trailed 1-0 at halftime before Mourinho made a triple substitution -- including the introduction of Belling
items.text:
Jude Bellingham praised José Mourinho for helping him reach career-best form after the midfielder scored a stunning goal in Real Madrid's 5-1 comeback win over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.
Madrid trailed 1-0 at halftime before Mourinho made a triple substitution -- including the introduction of Bellingham -- and the home side then dominated, with Kylian Mbappé netting a brace, and Vinícius Júnior scoring his first Champions League goal this season.
Madrid are now top of the league phase table with 15 points after winning all five UCL matches so far, with a visit to Arsenal in their next European game on Dec. 9.
"Mourinho. Full stop," Bellingham told journalists at the Bernabéu, when asked to explain his outstanding form, with four goals in his last five club games. "I'm enjoying my football a lot. I love the coach, his staff, and my teammates help me a lot.
"That's why I'm playing well, because I have a lot of help."
Bellingham's goal in the 60th minute was a beauty, coming after he lifted the ball with his left foot, kept it up in the air with his right and used the outside of the same foot to curl a shot into the far corner.
Bellingham spoke to TNT Sports too. If we wanted to add a bit more on his goal, we could:
"I think so," Bellingham told TNT Sports, when asked if his goal was among the best of his career. "They're normally a lot closer, aren't they!? That one was a nice one.
"It looped up nicely and I thought I'd go with the outside of my boot. I'm not one for smashing the ball too hard. It was a nice moment."
JUDE BELLINGHAM, THAT IS FILTHY 🤯 Two juggles, then a finish with the outside of his boot 💥 Stream the #UCL on @paramountplus 📺 https://t.co/8OOMUS4izI
— CBS Sports Golazo ⚽️ (@CBSSportsGolazo) November 24, 2026
Bellingham was also asked if his displays with England at the World Cup -- where he scored seven goals playing behind Harry Kane -- had been the catalyst for his renewed goal threat.
"I don't know if it's because I'm playing as a number 10, it's having freedom," Bellingham said. " Freedom to move, to drop deep, to help build up, and to play higher up to finish.
"I think Mourinho has given me a lot of confidence. That's why I'm playing well, because I'm happy."
Madrid have now beaten Inter Milan, Roma, RB Leipzig, AEK Athens and PSV in the Champions League this season, despite some inconsistent performances.
"The second half was a question of mentality," Mourinho told Movistar. "We made changes, and Jude is a different player. He gives us what we didn't have in the first [half].
"It was a mental 'click.' In the first half we didn't find our rhythm, we didn't press, we didn't win duels."
Mourinho refused to reveal if he'd been angry with his players in the dressing room at halftime.
"The dressing room is like Vegas," the coach said. "What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas.
"We spoke. We're friends, and we spoke."
"Once again, the first half wasn't good," goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois said. "In modern football, if we don't all run and do what the manager asks of us, it's impossible, especially against a team that presses you man-to-man.
"With the clips [Mourinho] showed us on the screen at halftime, you could see we weren't doing things right. That changed our attitude."
Madrid, who are three points behind LaLiga leaders Barcelona, next play Alaves at the Bernabeu on Nov. 28.

items.title: Arteta questions 'how in hell' Arsenal didn't score more in Dortmund draw
items.summary:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta rued his side's failure to put Borussia Dortmund away as "unbelievable" after watching the Premier League champions create 30 shots before drawing 1-1 at the Emirates Stadium.
Viktor Gyökeres crashed in Arsenal's opener after 10 minutes of Tuesday's Champions League cont
items.text:
Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta rued his side's failure to put Borussia Dortmund away as "unbelievable" after watching the Premier League champions create 30 shots before drawing 1-1 at the Emirates Stadium.
Viktor Gyökeres crashed in Arsenal's opener after 10 minutes of Tuesday's Champions League contest, but for the second time in as many games, following their 2-2 draw at Newcastle, Arteta's men were unable to see out the victory after Maximilian Beier's second-half equalizer.
Olley: Dortmund draw shows that the jury is still out on Gyökeres
Arsenal hit a post three times in response, while Gyökeres also wasted a golden opportunity to restore his side's advantage when he headed wide from six yards with 15 minutes left. In all, Arsenal found the target just four times.
Although Arteta was pleased with his side's dominant display, against a team that occupies top spot in the Bundesliga, he was left to reflect on what might have been.
"It was a brilliant performance," he said. "The way we played, bearing in mind the opposition, is something I can be very, very pleased about because there is very little more that you can demand from the team.
"But obviously, the feeling is we should reward ourselves much more when you put in that kind of performance and get those amount of chances.
"There is an element of luck, and an element of us finishing the actions better. There's no question how superior, how dominant, and how much of a threat we were. It was great to watch, but it was unbelievable that sometimes the ball didn't end up in the back of the net.
"I don't know if it is our mentality. As I said, there was an element of luck, because how in hell have some of the goals not gone in?"
The draw extended last season's finalists' unbeaten streak in the Champions League to 20 games but ended their 12-game home winning streak in league phase.
Arsenal now sit in fifth position ahead of the completion of the fifth round of matches on Wednesday. The top eight qualify automatically for the round of 16.
Tuesday saw goalkeeper Kepa Arrizabalaga handed a rare appearance in place of David Raya.
Arteta is uncertain if his number one -- injured against Newcastle on Saturday -- will be fit to face Manchester City in the Premier League this weekend.
"I have nothing to add to that unfortunately," he said. "We need to know first how bad it is and whether he has a chance or not to make it."
Arsenal might have had the lion's share of shots, but Jobe Bellingham had a goal ruled out for offside for Dortmund. Gyökeres could also count himself fortunate not to give away a penalty when a Dortmund corner struck him on the arm in the second half.
"I thought VAR should have looked at the handball. It would have been worth a check," Dortmund coach Niko Kovac said.
"They are trying to intervene less with the on-field decisions, but it doesn't mean you should not intervene when you should do.
"I am not crying about it. It is what it is. We got a point. It is a big point away to Arsenal, a big one for all of us -- our fans, our team and the club."
Information from PA contributed to this report.

Ukraine seeks €115 billion in foreign aid for 2027, Zelensky says
Ukraine will need €115 billion in external financing next year to sustain its economy and war effort against Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, adding that Kyiv had secured commitments for about €90 billion from the European Union.
Ukraine will need €115 billion ($125 billion) in external financial support in 2027, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday.
Zelensky told his top regional officials that the government had already secured about €90 billion in commitments from the European Union for the next year and was holding talks on where to find the remaining €25 billion.
With the war against Russia in its fifth year, Ukraine faces soaring war costs and depends on the military and financial support from Western allies to be able to stay in the fight.
The EU is now Ukraine's main financial supporter and last week it announced a plan to borrow another €45 billion to support Ukraine's economy and war effort.
Another €45 billion was part of €90 billion in financing approved in December last year and planned for this year and next.
"The European Commission has already presented a way to secure this funding, and we are now working to ensure that the European Union supports it," Zelensky said.
"We need to find another €25 billion. I am confident that we will accomplish this task."
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

items.text:
Poll finds US voters want government to end Iran war regardless of terms
New survey finds that 55 percent of voters, including 80 percent of Democrats, want the Iran war brought to an end immediately.
A new poll has found that a majority of voters in the United States want an end to the US-Israel war on Iran immediately, even if it means accepting less favourable conditions.
Overall, 55 percent of those surveyed agreed with an “end to the war now, regardless of the terms”.
That number was even higher among Democrats and independents, who agreed with the statement at a rate of 80 percent and 59 percent, respectively. About 25 percent of Republicans said the same.
A majority of Democratic voters also supported steps to pressure the administration of President Donald Trump to stop the conflict.
Fifty-three percent of party members said they would favour Congress withholding funding for military operations, and 51 percent would back an “an Iran war-funding cutoff” in upcoming budget negotiations, even if the manoeuvre risked a government shutdown.
The numbers were published on Tuesday as part of the latest Critical Issues Poll, released by the University of Maryland and the research firm Ipsos.
Shibley Telhami, the poll’s principal investigator, said he was surprised by the level of support for ending the war, regardless of the terms.
“We knew that people were strongly opposed to this war and wanted it to end,” he told Al Jazeera in a phone call. “What we were less sure of is what they would be willing to accept to achieve this.”
The survey asked 1,022 US adults about their perspectives on the war.
In one question, they were tasked with assessing with three options: whether to end the conflict immediately, escalate militarily, or continue on the current path in order to extract concessions from Iran.
Just 21 percent of all respondents favoured the current path, and 18 percent supported escalation.
“Clearly, the public mood is to end it now, whatever it takes,” said Telhami.
Questioning the rationale for war
Voters also appear sceptical about the US government’s arguments in favour of the war, which include dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme.
The Critical Issues Poll found that only 28 percent of those surveyed believed that the war had left Iran in “worse position” to develop nuclear weapons.
While the US has long voiced concerned that Iran could pursue nuclear arms, intelligence assessments have not found evidence that Tehran has authorised such a step since abandoning its nuclear weapons programme in 2003.
The Strait of Hormuz has also emerged as a key issue, with Iran closing the waterway to commercial traffic early in the war. The Trump administration has responded with a naval blockade in the strait.
Some 20 percent of the world’s oil supply passes through the maritime artery, and fuel prices have spiked as a result of the war.
About 35 percent of respondents in Tuesday’s poll said that they believe Iran is now in control of the strait, while just 12.7 percent said the US is in control.
The poll comes as the Democratic Party is debating how far it should go to end the unpopular war.
In the recent midterm elections, backlash against the war — and as well as related issues like rising fuel prices — contributed to big gains for the Democratic Party.
Trump’s Republican Party, meanwhile, suffered one of its most bruising setbacks in modern US history, losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Members of the Democratic Party’s anti-war left have pointed to the results as proof that voters want an end to the war and an end to US support for Israel.
But that position has brought them into conflict with members of the party’s more hawkish establishment wing.
While leaders such as Representative Hakeem Jeffries and Senator Chuck Schumer have both expressed support for ending the war, they have yet to commit to aggressive strategies to reach that goal.
That includes potentially cutting off funding for military operations against Iran, or using an upcoming funding battle in December to demand that the White House end the war.
“A lot of Democratic figures are dismissing the intensity of public feeling on this issue,” said Telhami. “If they don’t adapt, they will be left behind.”
He added that progressive figures such as Senator Bernie Sanders and Senator Chris Van Hollen have been among those pressing for a more assertive stance.
Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer to lead the Democratic majority in the US Senate, has used the war to portray the party’s moderate leadership as out of step with voters.
The poll found that Democratic voters prefer Van Hollen over Schumer by a ratio of nearly three to one.

items.text:
The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
- Published
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data, external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.
With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall, external, India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.
"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
The numbers bear this out.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.
In urban India, the corresponding rates were 6.1% and 5.3%.
The pressure is visible even in the cost of a simple meal.
Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis, external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.
Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.
And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
The rabi crop - winter crops, sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring - which accounts for roughly two-thirds of onion production, is harvested in March and April and stored for several months. As stocks dwindle, prices can rise sharply before the next crop arrives.
Tomatoes, meanwhile, tend to see price spikes during the summer months, when arrivals decline in some markets or heat stress affects production.
Sharma says perishables are often responsible for the sudden spikes in food inflation, while prices of staples such as rice and wheat tend to rise more gradually but can stay higher for longer.
"The perishables are what caused the volatility. The non-perishables, like rice and wheat, are the ones that structurally increase the cost," he says.
Economists say India still lacks adequate infrastructure to sort, grade, store and process much of its perishable produce.
Tomatoes, for example, can become so abundant during a glut that farmers struggle to sell them at remunerative prices, only for consumers to face sharply higher prices months later.
Better storage and processing could help turn some of that surplus into products such as puree, smoothing the extremes between abundance and scarcity, according to Sharma
There are other pressures.
Energy shocks feed into the cost of transport, irrigation and agricultural inputs. Fertiliser prices can rise. Global edible-oil markets matter because India relies heavily on imports.
To be true, India, however, has some protection against the worst effects of food inflation.
Government stocks of cereals are comfortably above prescribed minimum levels, and the free-food programme covering nearly 800 million people offers a cushion against rising prices. Rice stocks, external are particularly ample.
There is a wider economic risk, says Sengupta.
"Food inflation may begin with a supply shock, but its effects can spread. Workers who find that their wages no longer cover basic living costs may seek higher pay. Businesses facing higher labour costs may raise prices. What begins as a rise in the price of food can gradually become a more general inflationary pressure - the familiar wage-price spiral that central banks try to prevent," she says.
For India, this creates a particularly difficult balancing act.

items.text:
Shot in the face at 15: The lives shattered by Cameroon's decade of conflict
- Published
Median Bah was just 15 when her life changed forever.
She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed.
Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict.
Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately.
He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy.
"Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC.
That decision would have devastating consequences.
She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her.
They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face.
"I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls.
Everything went dark. She lost consciousness and could neither see nor speak.
Median initially thought she was dreaming.
"To my surprise, it was reality."
The attack left her with devastating facial injuries. Her jawbone was damaged, most of her teeth destroyed and much of her mouth severely injured.
Over the past eight years, she has undergone at least four reconstructive surgeries in Cameroon, Ghana and India, with more procedures expected next year.
Parts of her face have been reconstructed using tissue taken from other parts of her body.
She also lost the ability to breathe normally through her nose and mouth. She underwent a tracheostomy, a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck to allow air into the windpipe.
For eight years, she relied on a tube to breathe. It was only recently removed, allowing her to breathe normally again.
A teenager left with devastating facial injuries, a mother forced to flee her home and a student whose education was disrupted. Nearly a decade of fighting in Cameroon has left countless lives shattered.
The crisis began in October 2016, when lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's English-speaking regions went on strike over the alleged marginalisation of Anglophone communities by the Francophone-dominated government.
They were concerned about the appointment of French-speaking judges and teachers to courts and schools in the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions.
Initially, the protest was peaceful, with thousands demanding greater recognition of the English-speaking minority.
But human rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force to suppress the protests. The crackdown, critics say, helped fuel an armed separatist movement.
By 2017, a dozen armed groups had emerged, according to the International Crisis Group, seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions and the creation of a breakaway state known as Ambazonia.
Since then, separatist fighters have engaged in a prolonged and often brutal conflict with government forces.
Rights groups have documented serious abuses by both sides.
Separatist fighters have been accused of targeted killings, kidnappings for ransom, torture and attacks on schools and other public and private facilities.
Government forces, meanwhile, have faced allegations of arbitrary arrests and detention, torture and unlawful killings.
Both sides have denied the accusations, although in some instances they have acknowledged responsibility for abuses.
The violence has devastated communities and forced half a million people from their homes, according to data published by the UN this year.
At least 6,000 people have been killed since the conflict began, according to Human Rights Watch.
The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says more than 70,000 Cameroonians have sought refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.
Glory Akom, 44, lives with a disability after surviving severe burns in an incident unrelated to the conflict.
The mother-of-two now lives in a camp in Ogoja, a town in Nigeria's south-eastern Cross River state, near the Cameroonian border.
Ogoja hosts about 15,000 refugees across three settlements, Richard Effiong, from the UNHCR, told the BBC.
The UNHCR has provided refugees with brick houses topped with tin roofs.
For many, however, uncertainty remains over when, or whether, they will ever return home.
Glory says her life in Cameroon was far better. She ran a business and was able to provide for her family.
But everything changed when fighting intensified in 2017.
She said soldiers deployed to her area in the Southwest region pursued residents into the bush, forcing them to abandon their homes and flee into Nigeria.
"We were sleeping in the bush, as we were always running," she said.
"If you slept in your house, they could kill you there."
Initially, she settled in a neighbouring village before moving to Ogoja, where she was eventually allocated a permanent home.
Like many other refugees, Glory depends on $67 (£51) monthly cash assistance from UNHCR to support her children, one of who suffers from sickle cell and requires regular medical attention.
The money is barely enough to cover food, medical bills and other necessities, she says.
Her sadness at having to leave home is shared by other Cameroonian refugees in Ogoja who spoke to the BBC.
Maurine Mangha, 21, said she and five other members of her family fled Akwaya in the Southwest region after separatist fighters opened fire during celebrations marking what they described as their independence on 1 October 2017.
"They shot a lot of people, and we had no choice but run into the bush," she tells the BBC.
Maurine had stopped attending school months earlier because of a separatist-imposed education boycott.
The 2017 boycott campaign, which sought to pressure the government, involved threats and attacks against schools and those who defied orders to stay away.

items.summary:
