items.summary: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and
items.text:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”
In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads.
It’s not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Neither Adobe nor the NYT immediately responded to The Verge’s request for more information.

items.title: 2028 Copa América to be played in United States with six Concacaf teams
items.summary:
The 2028 Copa América will be played in the United States and expanded to include teams from the Concacaf region, bringing the landmark South American international competition to the US for a third time in five editions.
Conmebol, the South American confederation that runs the tournament, and Conca
items.text:
The 2028 Copa América will be played in the United States and expanded to include teams from the Concacaf region, bringing the landmark South American international competition to the US for a third time in five editions.
Conmebol, the South American confederation that runs the tournament, and Concacaf, the confederation governing soccer in North and Central America and the Caribbean, jointly announced the long-rumored arrangement on Tuesday, framing it as an extension of a “strategic partnership” between the organizations.
The tournament will be played from 9 June to 9 July 2028 – notably the same dates as Uefa’s European Championship, to be co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland. The 2028 summer Olympics will then follow in venues across the US, with the opening match of the men’s soccer tournament kicking off on 10 July, and the women’s tournament following the next day. The Olympic finals will land on the 28th (men’s) and 29th (women’s) of July.
The 2028 Copa América will involve 16 teams – all of Conmebol’s 10 member nations, along with six from Concacaf. The confederations announced that the Concacaf participants will be determined based on results at the 2027 Gold Cup, set to be played in the US in June and July next year. The exact qualification criteria have yet to be announced.
While the US’s large and growing appetite for soccer is part of the reason it has become a common landing spot for the Copa América over the last decade-plus, commercial considerations will also have been a major factor. The 2024 Copa América, which was also held in the US and involved six Concacaf teams, generated approximately $319m in revenue for Conmebol, the confederation said – a significant rise over the $118m generated by the 2019 edition in Brazil.
Argentina won the 2024 edition of the Copa América, with the final in Miami marred by ugly scenes of ticketless fans rushing the gates, causing injuries and damage to the stadium, delaying the start time by nearly 90 minutes. The previous edition hosted in the US, 2016’s Copa América Centenario, was won by Chile on penalties over Argentina at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.
As with that tournament, the 2024 Copa América and the 2026 World Cup, the 2028 tournament can be expected to be played largely in American football stadiums, most with capacities exceeding 60,000 people. But unlike those previous editions, the tournament will not overlap with Major League Soccer, thanks to the US league’s recent calendar flip.

items.title: Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
items.summary: Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether
items.text:
Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos autoplay.
The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta did when it announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.
But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.
This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.
Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.
Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.
The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

items.title: Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the gap with Nvidia in the AI chip race
items.summary: Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the r
items.text:
Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.
The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.
Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.
By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.
In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.
One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.
Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.
In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”
Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”

items.title: Manchester United win appeal over Yoro’s one-match suspension after Anfield red card
items.summary:

The Frenchman will no longer be required to ser
items.text:
Manchester United have successfully appealed against the decision to send off Leny Yoro in their 4-0 defeat to Liverpool. The defender was dismissed for denying an obvious goal scoring opportunity after eight minutes but this was found to be incorrect.
The Frenchman will no longer be required to serve a one-match suspicion. He fouled Liverpool’s Alexander Isak when through on goal in the early stages at Anfield but Mauricio Pochettino insisted the striker would not have reached the ball, and therefore is was not a sending off offence. The referee Sam Barrott made a different assessment, which the video assistant did not disagree with.
United’s head coach said: “I don’t agree because the ball wasn’t in Isak’s control. Leny was running with him and when Isak saw the control wasn’t good and the ball was going to the keeper it is normal you delay, you stop running, and you wait to feel the touch and you go down. It is never a foul.”
Dominik Szoboszlai scored the resulting free-kick, setting Liverpool on their way to victory to make it a difficult first match in charge for Pochettino. Yoro will now be available to face Brentford on Saturday in the Premier League.

Players Championship Finals 2026: Schedule and order of play as Gerwyn Price eyes another major title in Minehead
Gerwyn Price looks to back up his Grand Slam of Darts win by claiming a second straight major title; former champions Luke Humphries and Michael van Gerwen also among the 64-player field in Minehead, but world No 1 and defending champion Luke Littler did not qualify
Tuesday 24 November 2026 16:05, UK
The 2026 Ladbrokes Players Championship Finals sees 64 players competing to win the PDC's last major event before the World Darts Championship gets under way in December.
The tournament - which has a newly increased prize fund of £750,000 - features the top 64 ranked players following the conclusion of the 34-event Players Championship season, and takes place at Butlin's Minehead Resort from November 27-29.
Gerwyn Price, recently crowned Grand Slam of Darts champion for a fourth time, opens his bid for back-to-back major titles against Sebastian Bialecki on Friday, with record seven-time winner Michael van Gerwen in action against Connor Scutt and Luke Humphries - triumphant in 2023 and 2024 - going up against Darryl Pilgrim.
Top seed Wessel Nijman has been handed a tough opener against exciting youngster Henry Coates, while Beau Greaves makes her Players Championship Finals debut against Christian Kist.
World No 1 and defending champion Luke Littler did not qualify for the Finals.
Friday's first round winners advance to Saturday's double session, with the second round scheduled for the afternoon and round three in the evening.
The tournament concludes on Sunday November 29, with the afternoon's quarter-finals followed by the semi-finals and final in a decisive evening session that also includes the Winmau World Youth Championship final between Cam Crabtree and Jan Schmidt.

The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of t
items.text:
Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling
- Published
Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).
The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.
The result of that match in Rabat, which saw the Teranga Lions triumph 1-0 after extra time, was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed Senegal had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to Cas, sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.
In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners.
The court said it considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."
The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always".
Caf is yet to comment on the decision but its president Patrice Motsepe has repeatedly said that his organisation will respect and adhere to the Cas ruling.
Morocco's football federation (FRMF) is also yet to comment on the verdict.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final 
  - Published19 January
Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.
This ruling should now settle any debate about who the history books will recognise as continental champions - although plenty in Morocco may not agree with the outcome of the case at Cas.
What happened in the Afcon final?
A tightly-contested match between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Jean-Jacques Ndala at the centre of the drama.
First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.
The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.
Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Brahim Diaz back before heading a corner clear.
Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by VAR.
Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.
They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.
The game went into extra time, with midfielder Pape Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.
But, off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.
What was the fallout?
Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF quickly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.
It states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".
A disciplinary board from the continental game's governing body rejected the FRMF's protest days after the final as it sanctioned and fined those found guilty of unsporting conduct during the match.
Yet in March, almost two months on from the final, a Caf appeals board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.
The FSF described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and swiftly lodged its case with Cas.
The director general of the Switzerland-based court said arbitration proceedings would be conducted "as swiftly as possible", but it was over five months until all parties descended on Lausanne for a one-day hearing.
The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.
The FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.
Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.
But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.

items.text:
LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
5 min read
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?
Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.
So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.
It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks
Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.
So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone???
This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!
Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.
Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.
And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.
This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.
On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.
- And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. ↩︎

items.text:
Polymarket : Autopsie d'un délit d'initié sur la réintégration de Jensen Huang chez NVIDIA [!NOTE] Pourquoi cet article et cette analyse ? Depuis quelque temps, je constate que Polymarket devient un véritable terrain de jeu pour les délits d’initiés, et le climat politique autour de la nouvelle administration Trump rend ce type d’asymétrie d’information encore plus propice. J’ai donc développé un algorithme qui surveille en permanence les marchés les plus sensibles : chaque transaction y est analysée par des modèles statistiques et des outils de traçage de flux on-chain. J’ai finalisé l’algo il y a deux jours à peine. Dans la nuit même, en voyant l’alerte se déclencher, j’ai mené une première analyse à chaud sur les transactions… avant de voir tomber quelques heures plus tard le tweet de Donald Trump confirmant l’asymétrie. Et vous allez voir que le communiqué officiel de NVIDIA n’était que la cerise sur le gâteau. Cette enquête documente, à la minute et au hash près, un cas assez probant de délit d’initié sur Polymarket détecté en temps réel. Question principale Y a-t-il eu un délit d’initié sur le marché « Will Jensen Huang rejoin NVIDIA by December 31, 2026? » ? - Le timing : Une accumulation de liquidité achevée en pleine nuit Transactions Polygon, exactement 89 minutes avant la prise de position publique de Donald Trump sur Truth Social ; - L’asymétrie de gain : 4 648 USDC engagés sur une probabilité marginale de 6,5 %, dénoués en 71 518 USDC suite à la confirmation unanime du Conseil d’Administration de NVIDIA sur Polymarket ; - Le profil du portefeuille : Un compte jetable Gnosis Safe Proxy créé 81 heures auparavant, dont l’activité est 100 % monothématique. Question secondaire : En quoi les marchés de prédiction décentralisés constituent-ils désormais le sismographe le plus implacable pour révéler publiquement des délits d’initiés invisibles sur les bourses traditionnelles ? Réponse courte (avant d’entrer dans le détail) Sur le strict plan des données on-chain, l’hypothèse du hasard est statistiquement disqualifiée. L’acheteur anonyme opérant sous le pseudonyme ljhggk a méthodiquement balayé le carnet d’ordres jusqu’à 0,065 $, verrouillé sa position avant toute réaction de marché, puis encaissé passivement les deux catalyseurs successifs pour réaliser un gain net de +66 869,34 USDC (+1 438,5 % de ROI). flowchart TB subgraph Chronologie ["Reconstitution temporelle (Heure française CET)"] direction TB A["23/11 · 02:19 - 03:28 CET

Multiplicateur : 15,38x"] 1 · L’Anatomie du trade : 71 518 parts OTM raflées en pleine nuit Entre 02:19:11 et 03:28:20 CET (01:19 - 02:28 UTC) dans la nuit du dimanche au lundi 23 novembre 2026, le carnet d’ordres du marché Will Jensen Huang rejoin NVIDIA by December 31, 2026? était totalement assoupi. La probabilité implicite stagnait à 6,5 %, reflétant un consensus quasi-unanime : suite à sa démission du 12 novembre, un retour de Huang avant la fin de l’année paraissait exclu. C’est à cet instant précis qu’un acteur unique déploie une stratégie d’absorption agressive, découpée en 4 ordres limités successifs : Le relevé des 4 transactions sur Polygon Chaque transaction a été retracée. Les 4 transactions ont été incluses dans les blocs sans rejet Registre complet : [!NOTE] Verdict technique de l’exécution : L’opérateur n’a pas étalé ses achats sur 24 heures pour moyenner son coût. Il a exécuté un achat massif et concentré en pleine nuit européenne/américaine, absorbant 34 % de toute la liquidité vendeuse disponible sur le contrat, ce qui pourrait montrer qu’il a eu l’info quelques heures avant et qu’il n’a pas spécialement eu le temps de l’étaler davantage. Dès son dernier ordre complété à 03:28:20 CET, il s’est totalement arrêté de négocier. À noter : le compte s’était déjà positionné sur de petits montants sur ce pari dès sa création, mais sans jamais approcher de volumes comparables à ce qui a levé l’alerte cette nuit-là. Cette montée soudaine en conviction renforce encore la suspicion. 2 · La Reconstitution temporelle : 89 minutes d’avance sur le monde réel Le cœur du dossier réside dans la corrélation temporelle entre la clôture de l’accumulation on-chain et la chaîne des déclarations publiques. 02:19 CET ─── 03:28 CET ──────── 04:57 CET ────────────────────── 14:30 CET ─── 15:40 CET [Achats] [Fin Accum.] [Post Trump] [PR NVIDIA] [Résolution] 4 648 $ Verrouillé « I hope the Board... » Officiel 1.00 $ 71 518 parts Truth Social Wall Street 71 518 $ ▲ │ │ └──── +89 min ─────┘ │ └────────────────────── +11h 02min ────────────────┘ 1. Le catalyseur politique : La publication de Donald Trump (+89 min) À 04:57:00 CET (22:57:00 EST le 22 novembre), Donald Trump publie sur son réseau Truth Social : « I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. » Il ne s’agit pas d’une injonction légale, mais le poids politique est massif : la mise à l’écart de Huang reposait sur des craintes de sécurité nationale. Le soutien explicite de Trump lève immédiatement le principal verrou psychologique. Le contrat bondit instantanément de 0,065 $ à 0,14 $ dans les échanges de la nuit. 2. items.text:
Searching for distant planets with Astra
Two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely.
Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system(opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992(opens in a new window). A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers.
Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope(opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90(opens in a new window).
Now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars.
Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission.
One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit shows up as a dip. If the dip keeps coming back at regular intervals, astronomers know when to watch for it again.
Searching for that pattern across thousands of stars is partly a coding problem. Astronomers have published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips in years of measurements. Bond used Codex to compare those methods, combine them in a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved the search. One AI agent scanned the light curves for promising signals. Another ran more detailed checks on the candidates the first one flagged.
Bond ran the program on public data from the Kepler Space Telescope. The search flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets. Finding those known planets gave Bond confidence that the program could pick out the kinds of signals he was looking for.
Two stars stood out. The first, KIC 5689121, is a relatively cool star about half the size of our sun in the constellation Lyra. The Codex search found a dip in brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing it, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times Earth’s diameter.
The second star, KIC 6691030, is faint and lies in the northern sky. The Codex search found a dip in its brightness every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune. These were the two signals the SETI Institute astronomer found independently. Confirming what caused them could take months or years.
“Kevin’s work shows how citizen scientists, equipped with AI, can help astronomers explore the Kepler Bonus Catalog—a vast collection of stars beyond Kepler’s original targets. His pipeline has surfaced promising candidates in data traditional searches may have missed. Our initial checks are encouraging, and follow-up observations will tell us more.”
Byrd used Astra to design two searches. One looked broadly for exoplanet candidates. The other focused on stars’ habitable zones. A habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface.
Byrd then asked Astra to review published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals. His searches drew on observations from TESS, which NASA launched in 2018, and from other public telescope archives.
The first pass through the data turned up 49 candidates. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on the TESS mission, where it is awaiting further analysis. His search is still running.
When astronomers see a star dim, they have to consider what else might explain it. Two stars passing in front of one another can produce a similar dip. Even a change in temperature aboard a telescope can affect its instruments enough to make a star appear to dim.
Astronomers can use statistics to show that an exoplanet is the most likely explanation for a series of dips. They can also collect more observations, sometimes using a different method. For example, an orbiting planet’s gravity tugs on its star, causing it to move slightly toward and away from us. That motion, called radial velocity, shows up as tiny shifts in the color of the star’s light. Astronomers then publish their findings in a peer-reviewed journal so others can examine the evidence.

items.text:
DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
- Published
The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.
On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a warplane that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.
Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.
The BBC has not independently verified the rebels' claim.
It is also unclear whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one rebels say they shot down.
Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.
- What's the fighting in DR Congo all about? 
  - Published5 December 2025
- How former President Kabila became FRN rebel leader 
  - Published31 October
A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."
The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.
Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".
Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.
In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.
He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.
South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".
"Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.
In 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.
The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.
In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.
The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.
Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.
Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.
The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

items.title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
items.summary:
Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
- Published
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to dro
items.text:
Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
- Published
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.
Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.
After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.
There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women
In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."
He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.
The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."
Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.
Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.
Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempto

items.title: Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
items.summary:
Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the wat
items.text:
Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
- Published
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
- Can Nigeria's president regain voters' trust after painful first term? 
  - Published12 November
- Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy 
  - Published41 minutes ago
Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.
The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.
Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.
In 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.
"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,” he said.
Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (£1.5bn) investment in a new East–West Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.
Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

items.title: Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case
items.summary:
Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes, but the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations has been playing out for 10 months.
Now, finally, Morocco or Senegal will be crowned winners. However, that moment of glo
items.text:
Morocco and Senegal await Afcon final verdict after court case
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes, but the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations has been playing out for 10 months.
Now, finally, Morocco or Senegal will be crowned winners. However, that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Tuesday afternoon sport's highest legal authority, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), will render its judgement on Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they won in January against the hosts in Rabat.
The case was heard in early October, and the wait is almost over.
So how did we get here?
What happened in the Afcon final?
With 66,000 fans creating an electric atmosphere in the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco were chasing their first Afcon title since 1976.
But the final descended into chaos deep into second-half stoppage time.
With the match goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had blown for a Morocco free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a video assistant referee (VAR) review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.
Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
The Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing that Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled 'Withdrawals', states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team... refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee", they shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, some people, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The FSF's appeal was heard in private on 8 October by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
The panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas completed the trio.
If the panel had failed to come to a consensus on the case, Cas president Simon will have made the final decision.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Although Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said in March that it will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so, if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Senegal walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw lost his job following Senegal's last-32 World Cup exit this summer, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Morocco dugout in January, was dismissed in March.
Whatever the outcome of the case, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy was furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked Senegal, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf b

items.title: Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy
items.summary:
Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy
- Published
Search and rescue operations are racing against time in Nigeria after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesper
items.text:
Search and rescue teams race against time after Nigeria boat tragedy
- Published
Search and rescue operations are racing against time in Nigeria after a boat carrying mourners travelling to a funeral capsized on Friday.
Twenty-nine bodies have been recovered and 50 people rescued so far, a spokesperson for the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) told the BBC.
The government has responded by ordering stricter enforcement of safety standards on the country's inland waterways.
Overcrowding, poor maintenance and failure to observe safety regulations have contributed to previous deadly accidents on Nigeria's rivers.
The boat was travelling from Ayama community when it developed mechanical problems, according to police spokesperson Musa Mohammed.
Passengers asked the boat operator to steer towards land, but he allegedly declined, leading to the accident.
Survivors have described the panic that followed as passengers struggled to swim and stay afloat while waiting for emergency rescue services.
"As I swam, people were dragging me to the bottom, and I bit one woman and saved myself," Charity Ebikaboaere told local media outlet Arise News.
"Our things, our money, phones, everything lost, but me and my siblings are alive," said another survivor, Tari Samuel.
- Why do Nigeria's boat disaster keep happening? 
  - Published20 July
Nema spokesman Manzo Ezekiel raised concerns about the use of untrained boat operators and passengers travelling without life jackets.
"Some of them believe they're from river areas and they know how to swim," he said, warning that familiarity with waterways should not replace basic safety precautions.
The accident happened in a region where waterways are a key means of transport, especially for communities with limited road access.
"Overloading, speeding, recklessness and traveling without life jackets must stop. No journey is worth a life," Bayelsa Commissioner for Information Ebiuwou Koku-Obiyai said in a statement on Saturday.
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu has relayed his condolences to the victims' families.
In a statement posted on X, Tinubu said he had directed relevant federal disaster response agencies to work together to ensure a successful rescue and recovery operation.
He also ordered that his election rally on Saturday, in Ibadan, Oyo State, be held without much fanfare in honour of those who lost their lives.
Boat accidents are a recurring problem in Nigeria, particularly in riverine communities where boats are a major means of transport.
In August, at least 50 people, mostly children, died after an overloaded boat capsized in the north-western Sokoto state. In January, at least 25 people died when a leaking boat capsized in Yobe state, in the north-east.

items.title: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
items.summary:
Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of
items.text:
Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
- Published
Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.
Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.
This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.
On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".
The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.
Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".
DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).
DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.
DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.
When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.
The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.
DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.
- Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader 
  - Published31 October
Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.
Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.
He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.
Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.
The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.
On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.
Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.
More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

items.text:
Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
- Published
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.
The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X., external
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."
If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman and Shayan Sardarizadeh

items.text:
Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
- Published
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.
At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.
He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.
"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.
But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.
Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.
The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.
His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.
Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).
Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.
The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.
In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".
His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.
But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.
"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.
The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.
Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.
But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.
Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.
But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.
Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.
"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.
The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.
Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.
Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.
Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.
This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.
But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.
Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.
"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.
Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.
For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.
Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.
The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.
Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.
The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.
The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; £56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.
Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.
These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.
Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.
The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.
Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.
"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.
Fatima Zahra Umar, a young politician in the APC who has previously tried to run for a seat in the House of Representatives, agrees.

items.text:
Ireland beat world champions South Africa in thriller
- Published
Nations Championship
Ireland (17) 20
Tries: Baloucoune 2, Kelleher Con: Prendergast Pen: Prendergast
South Africa (10) 17
Try: Van den Berg, Marx Cons: Feinberg-Mngomezulu 2 Pens: Feinberg-Mngomezulu
Ireland exacted revenge on world champions South Africa with a thrilling win in Dublin after England's victory over New Zealand dashed Andy Farrell's side's hopes of reaching next weekend's Nations Championship final.
With banned South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus hosting a watchalong stream from his team's hotel, the Springboks fell to back-to-back Test defeats for the first time since November 2022 after last week's loss to France in Paris.
A losing bonus-point, however, is enough for South Africa to top the southern hemisphere table and secure a place in the final against France, who beat Argentina 45-17 later on Saturday.
Ireland, who were shown five cards during last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, led at the break after two tries from Robert Baloucoune and a Ronan Kelleher score, with Morne van den Berg crossing for the visitors.
After Canan Moodie had a try ruled out early in the second half, Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast - who was cleared to play by a disciplinary panel earlier this week - stretched Ireland's lead with a penalty.
However, hooker Malcolm Marx's 57th-minute try hauled South Africa back into it before yellow cards for Ireland captain Dan Sheehan and Springbok replacement Marco van Staden - the latter upgraded to red - set up a nail-biting denouement in the final 10 minutes.
But amid a hair-raising atmosphere inside Aviva Stadium, Ireland held on for a much-needed win after six successive double-digit defeats by the Springboks, New Zealand and France.
France's win meant that Ireland had to settle for third place in the table, and they will face Australia in a fifth-place play-off at Twickenham on Friday at 20:10 GMT.
Ireland narrowly beat Australia 33-31 in Sydney in July, but the Wallabies have since had a change of head coach after Les Kiss replaced Joe Schmidt.
Ireland front up to SA after Erasmus-dominated build-up
After an explosive build-up headlined by Erasmus, who was banned for six matches on Tuesday after questioning the integrity of match officials in last week's game against France, Saturday's contest in Dublin had a lot to live up to.
But it delivered emphatically during a breathless first half as Ireland fronted up impressively to South Africa's immense physicality.
In last year's meeting in Dublin, Ireland ended a nightmarish first half with 12 players on the field as South Africa - and their mighty scrum - played the game on their terms.
Fuelled by the pain of that encounter, Ireland attacked the game with real gusto and while South Africa fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu kicked the first points of the game, Ireland bossed possession and territory for much of the opening half.
There were plenty of moments for the sold-out crowd to cheer, with perhaps the biggest roar reserved for the hosts winning a rare scrum penalty after 26 minutes.
Baloucoune was exceptional, too. In addition to faring well in the aerial battle, the rapid Ulster wing displayed his finishing skills to get Ireland on the board, slipping past Damian Willemse and touching down after being picked out by Stuart McCloskey.
While Baloucoune - who also crossed twice against Fiji last week - was denied a second try by a superb piece of last-ditch defending by Springbok number eight Cameron Hanekom, Joe McCarthy won a turnover to deny the visitors momentum.
From there, Ireland kicked to the corner and eventually worked the ball back to Baloucoune on the right, who dived over in the corner for his second.
But with both conversion attempts missed by Prendergast, Ireland were pegged back when South Africa won a penalty inside green territory, with Van den Berg dotting down off the back of a scrum.
Unlike last year, though, Ireland had the final say of the half and restored their lead when Kelleher scored off a well-worked line-out.
South Africa's frustration deepened early in the second half when Moodie's fine finish in the corner was ruled out after the replacement back was pushed into touch by Mack Hansen.
Ireland pulled further clear when Prendergast atoned for his missed kicks at goal with a penalty to put the hosts 20-10 up.
But after world player of the year Marx forced his way over with more than 20 minutes remaining, Ireland were denied a fourth try when Sheehan - in his first Test start at number eight - was held up on the line.
Sheehan was then yellow-carded at the same time as Van Staden, for a croc roll and dangerous clear-out respectively, and while South Africa pushed for a late winner, Ireland held on for a statement win.
Reacting from what looked like a conference room at his team's hotel, Erasmus slammed a table in frustration at full-time before his stream ended, spelling a miserable end to a tumultuous week for the two-time World Cup-winning coach.
Line-ups
Ireland: Keenan; Baloucoune, Henshaw, McCloskey, Hansen; Prendergast, Gibson-Park; Porter, Kelleher, Furlong, McCarthy, Beirne, Baird, Van der Flier, Sheehan (capt)
